subsubtopic: INTERFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the very serious crash landing of a T.C.A. plane at Malton airport last night, and the disturbing report attributed to radar operators that practice attempts in the United States to jam Russian radar screens are fouling up commercial radarscopes at the airport, can the minister say whether such jamming contributed to this crash and whether the Canadian government has objected to the United States that the operation of the Canadian commercial radarscope at Malton airport is being interfered with?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: INTERFERENCE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. I understand that in this accident the plane went off the end of the runway after touching down, but I am not in any position to comment on the causes of the accident. Both departmental and air line investigators are already at work looking into the situation, and this inquiry will be -carried forward.
With regard to the hon. member's reference to the jamming of Malton radar, it is known that theoretically United States military exercises in radar jamming within the boundaries of the United States might in some circumstances interfere with Canadian air traffic control operations which are located close to the United States boundary, but in fact this has not happened.
This situation is being kept under review, and should anything serious develop there exist in the standing arrangements for consultation between my department and the United States federal aviation agency adequate channels through which this type of problem can be dealt with.

subsubtopic: INTERFERENCE
speechtext:
A supplementary question. I wonder whether the minister would care to tell the house whether the report in the Montreal Gazette this morning is correct, which states:
Radar operators at suburban Malton airport reported to the federal transport department that-

subsubtopic: INTERFERENCE
speechtext:

take place; but, if the hon. member was listening, I said that in fact this has not happened.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made this morning by the President of the United States of a new proposal-which will be discussed at the nuclear conference of three powers now under way in Geneva-together with the speech yesterday by Chairman Khrushchev to the

parliament of India in Delhi, emphasize the relevancy and the urgency of the position Canada should take in this all-important question, to use the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs disarmament.
The President's statement as announced this morning is that the United States is proposing to end forthwith, under assured controls, all nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, in the oceans, in those regions in space where effective controls can now be agreed on, and beneath the surface of the earth in cases where they can be monitored. Then the President made a significant observation, when he said the achievement of a workable nuclear test ban was by far the most important and difficult beginning to be made on the general subject of disarmament.
It is interesting to note that the position taken by Canada with regard to the unqualified banning of tests is to be contrasted in part with the proposal announced by the President of the United States, I do not need to spend needless time in justification of the consideration of disarmament in this debate.
I formed the impression after reading the minister's remarks this morning that, unintentionally, I am sure, he did convey the impression that this government was concerned with disarmament as its foremost objective. He also left the impression that not much had been done in this field in the period immediately preceding the time when hon. gentlemen opposite took over the responsibility of government in Canada.
That, of course, would be a wrong impression for anyone to have, because it will be recalled that almost at the very end of the war Canada and the government of that day, together with the friendly associated powers, did take immediate and comprehensive steps to bring about a solution to the problem of atomic armaments. In 1945 the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada offered to reciprocally share information concerning the practical application of atomic energy as soon as effective safeguards were devised against its use for destructive purposes. It will be remembered that at the first meeting of the United Nations Canada was made a member of the atomic energy commission. Following this joint declaration by the three heads of government, including Canada, there was presented a comprehensive, a most selfless plan for disarmament, and particularly nuclear disarmament, by the United States through Mr. Baruch, as the intermediary in the atomic energy commission.
It is important to remember what that proposal was. It suggested an international atomic development authority to which-
-would be entrusted all phases of the development and use of atomic energy, starting with the
External Affairs
raw material, with managerial control or ownership of all atomic energy activities potentially dangerous to world security, and power to control, license and inspect all other atomic activities, and which should itself be the world leader in the field of atomic knowledge and development so as to enable it to comprehend and therefore detect misuse of atomic energy.
The record now demonstrates that the Soviet union rejected this proposal and countered with one of its own, in which it was insisted that there should be an immediate prohibition of the use, production and accumulation of atomic weapons. That remained until 1954 the cardinal principle of Soviet policy on disarmament. There can be no doubt that the failure to make any progress in disarmament until 1955 was due, in my judgment, to the intransigence of the Soviet union with regard to this proposal and to its subsequent modifications, and other later proposals made by the western powers.
After 1955 the Soviet union did agree to a measure of international inspection and control, but never in specific and definable terms. The house will recall, too, that in 1954 the United Nations decided to create a subcommittee of the disarmament commission. As an indication of the interest Canada took in disarmament at that time, to the United States, Great Britain, France and the Soviet union as members of that committee was added the name of Canada.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) took part in the initial work of that subcommittee. If the subcommittee did not succeed-and it did not-the fault certainly was not that of Canada. The fault, generally speaking, was not that of the west, although I must say in an effort to be objective that the fault does not entirely rest on the Soviet union from that period on.
It is significant that France and Great Britain put forward at one of the early meetings of the subcommittee a comprehensive proposal for disarmament, a plan known as the Anglo-French plan. It was a three-stage disarmament scheme providing for a freeze on military establishments, in the first phase; for a second phase including the first half of agreed reductions in conventional forces and arms plus a cut-off on the production of nuclear weapons, and a final phase which was to see the completion of the remaining half of the agreed reductions of conventional arms. This was to be followed-and this was an answer to the Soviet union-by total prohibition and elimination of all nuclear weapons, and the conversion of all stocks to peaceful uses.
That memorandum represents one of the important landmarks in the discussions on disarmament. This Anglo-French initiative

External Affairs
was rejected by the Soviet union. It was supported by the United States and by Canada as members of the subcommittee.
In 1954 the then permanent delegate at the United Nations, Mr. Andre Vishinsky, made an important statement when he announced in the general assembly that the Soviet union had altered its traditional attitude. No longer would it insist on a ban on the manufacture and use and accumulation of atomic weapons as a condition precedent to entering into efforts to reach a solution on disarmament. And as a further evidence of the position of Canada in these discussions, the recognition of the useful role she had pursued, Canada was selected by the United States, France and Great Britain to carry on negotiations with the Soviet union which led to a resolution that stood in the name of the five powers and received the unanimous endorsa-tion of the general assembly of the United Nations.
Last night the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the resolution on disarmament put forward by the five great powers at the last assembly received unanimous support by all the United Nations, and he interpreted that as an indication of hope for the future.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out to the hon. member that I said it was cosponsored by all 82 nations.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. I do not want to be unfair to what my hon. friend said, but I would suggest that if that was an achievement-and it was merely a procedural resolution-so too was the achievement of 1954. But the significant point is that there was no constructive result arising from the unanimity. We should not draw unwarranted conclusions from unanimity on procedural resolutions, asserting that as a result we have cause to think we are now entering a more successful chapter in disarmament discussions. I hope we are, but I think it is well for us to curb our optimism with realism and give careful scrutiny to steps that may be taken which may represent more form than substance. Let us hope that the situation is otherwise.
It seems to me the next important step was the summit meeting in Geneva in 1954, when President Eisenhower, Sir Anthony Eden and Prime Minister Faure of France confronted Mr. Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev and when, as the result of a week's talk, four proposals on disarmament were put forward.
I would again suggest to hon. members that the spirit of Geneva that flowed from that summit meeting, giving hope as it did to all of the peoples of the world, has its counterpart

in the kind of possible false hope that could ensue as a result of discussions now under way. We must not be misled by generalizations of any kind. In our efforts to bring about disarmament we must recognize the value of a healthier international climate, but before giving final judgment we must see whether or not we have the acceptance of positions which we think are necessary for the maintenance of our security and for the successful pursuit of our objectives in the field of disarmament.
At this summit meeting a number of proposals were made, and for my present purposes the significant one was that put forward by President Eisenhower. He said to Mr. Khrushchev and Mr. Bulganin, "It is now scientifically impossible to detect undisclosed or secret nuclear weapons. You admitted that in discussions in the subcommittee only a few weeks ago. That being the case, since we cannot at present have full control on disarmament I make a proposal to you. Let us exchange our military blueprints. Let each give the other the opportunity of carrying out an aerial inspection survey in the territory of the other". The Soviet union did not accept that proposal. Canada was the one country, recognizing the scientific fact and the desirability of creating a, healthier international atmosphere, that did give support in principle to the Eisenhower proposal.
I think it is significant to note that as a result of the four-power meeting the subcommittee were instructed by the heads of the four governments to resume their discussions. They did not decide anything on disarmament. That was left once again to the subcommittee. It will be remembered that the subcommittee had its first meeting after the summit meeting on August 14, 1955. It will be remembered, too, that in September of that year the President of the United States suffered a serious heart seizure. From that moment on the Geneva spirit disappeared or dissipated. From that time forward there was no evidence of any progress, in spite of the good intentions and the healthy atmosphere that prevailed at the meetings in Geneva.
Canada at that time took a position, one that reflected the independence of Canada in foreign policy, as a result of the initiative and the character given that policy by the present Leader of the Opposition. We took the position that because we were apparently not able to resolve any of our differences, if we could not agree on some measure of disarmament on existing weapons, conventional or nuclear, could we not try to arrive at some agreement with respect to weapons

which were not then in existence? We of course had reference to the intercontinental ballistic missile.
It is not the fault of Canada-the record is there for everyone to see-that even more terrible weapons of war now confront us on an increasingly alarming scale. If our point of view had been pursued and accepted by all concerned it is possible that we would not be talking today of missiles that are capable of bringing about even greater destruction than other instruments of war.
This is perhaps what the Prime Minister was thinking about when at the general assembly in 1957 he said:
Experience has taught us that no country ever possesses a monopoly on any device. What one country has today, the other nations will have tomorrow, and the day is not far distant, if this continues, when there will be armouries of these rockets.
So we did take this position, even though it was a position which we alone took. We took another position. Because of the statement made by the President about the scientific fact precluding the complete control of undetected nuclear weapons, the United States reserved its position on all matters to which it had given its support up to that time. I -have referred to the Anglo-French memorandum of March, 1954 which was, apart from the Baruch plan, the first comprehensive proposal. The United States, through Mr. Harold Stassen, on September 6, 1955 stated:
The United States does now place a reservation upon all of its pre-Geneva substantive positions taken in this subcommittee, or in the disarmament commission, or in the United Nations on these questions in relationship to levels of armament.
Canada sought to persuade her -close and friendly associate in these matters that this was an unnecessary position to take, but other members of the subcommittee also took this position. The result wat that the agreement on manpower ceilings, the disarmament program produced by Britain and France, the 50 per cent arrangement about the cutoff, the 75 per -cent arrangement about the elimination of nuclear stocks, the detailed plan for inspection and control were all withdrawn. I believe that was at that time an unnecessary step. The Soviet union certainly did not make matters easy by taking the position it did with regard to bases and the like. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there -can be no doubt that during all of this period Canada has pursued, I believe diligently, its policy of trying, in concert with -other countries, to bring about an agreement on disarmament.
There was no want of independence; there was no reluctance to take a responsible position when it had to be taken, and I suggest to the Secretary of State for External
External Affairs
Affairs that if this is the important matter he says it is in current international affairs, Canada will have to do more than rely on its popularity as -a substitute for policy. Canada will have to do more than make generalizations with regard to this important matter if it wants to make the kind of contribution which I believe all of us want Canada to make at this time; and I am sure "all of us" includes the hon. gentleman who spoke yesterday. But I complained yesterday -and I think with some right-that in a matter of this sort, having in mind the importance which the hon. member attaches to this problem, it was regrettable that the government did not put forward some of its proposals or, at least, the principles on which those proposals are based.
I mentioned that Great Britain had taken that course in September. Chairman Khrushchev outlined the Soviet union proposals. Today we have the President of the United States making a proposal with regard to the banning of tests and saying that this is an essential prerequisite to a comprehensive system of disarmament, or to a system of partial disarmament. There are other proposals, namely the proposals put forward the other day by the French government, in which they emphasized the importance of controlling -production and the means of delivery of nuclear weapons.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
whether he is suggesting that the French proposals to which he refers were detailed proposals in any way whatever?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I said they were detailed proposals in the sense in which the proposals of Mr. Khrushchev and the proposals of Mr. Lloyd were detailed proposals. They did not spell out every "i" and every semi-colon, but the proposals in main outline are there. What have we got from the hon. gentleman? I am saying this only because I do feel keenly about this subject, as I know he does; but all we have got from the hon. gentleman is his declaration-and I admit that is important-that he believes in disarmament; that the government believes in disarmament and intends to pursue the matter. All I am saying is that as an earnest, as a demonstration of his good intentions, we should have had from the hon. gentleman a statement that would at least outline the basic program or the basic principles of that program.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. gentleman whether he thinks it would help to attain the ultimate objective in those negotiations which are to take place between the east

External Affairs
and west if the Canadian government were to come in today and give in detail all its proposals before the negotiations commence?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in saying that the time has come when the west should seek to dominate the position in terms of influencing world public opinion on this subject. The way to do this is for the western powers not to hesitate to express their positions, as was done by the government of the United Kingdom on the floor of the assembly of the United Nations last September, and as was done from his point of view by Chairman Khrushchev at the same assembly. I say that Canada speaks not only for herself, as the minister acknowledged yesterday, but for a whole series of nations.
We are no less interested in disarmament than is Chairman Khrushchev, perhaps more so; yet he has been able, by the disclosure of the details of his proposals, to give the impression, particularly to the uncommitted peoples of the underdeveloped areas of the world, in Asia, that he more than anyone else is interested in disarmament, when the record clearly shows that the Soviet union has been more intransigent in this particular than any other country. Surely it would not be exposing our flank if the minister, in discussing this matter yesterday, had said that he concurs in the principles, for instance, in April 24, 1952 in the disarmament commission.
Are these principles still the policy of the government of Canada? We do not know. I have no doubt they are; I would find it very difficult to believe that they could not be; but those principles, setting out clearly the attitude which this country and other countries took, were not even referred to by the hon. gentleman yesterday. I can only assume that there would be no exposing of one's position by reciting principles that were referred to time and time again by spokesmen for Canada in discussions in the general assembly, in the main outlining principles which established our position in the matter of controls, our attitude on reductions in conventional forces, our attitude as to when there should begin a prohibition of atomic weapon use and manufacture.
Surely we are entitled to know whether these are still the principles. This is important, because apparently they no longer represent the principles to be adopted by France, particularly in the matter of nuclear weapons. Therefore it would be important -certainly it would be important for the people in India, for other people who have been influenced by what I think oftentimes on the part of the Soviet union has been propaganda-not	always-to convince those

people that the west is seriously dedicated to the prosecution of disarmament, in the hope that we can transfer tremendous sums of money for purposes of defence, and capable of being used for purposes of destruction, into constructive purposes of national development and health and welfare. There is so much involved in these principles that I want to say to the minister that he will find that unless he is prepared to give more than lip service to this question, we will not make the contribution which we should and which I know we want to make.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? I gather from the line of approach he is taking that he places chief reliance for the solution of the disarmament problem on some plan or other which may be produced by a particular nation, either of the west or of the east. Is the hon. member not aware that at the basis of disarmament plans lies the desire of establishing some measure of confidence between the west and the east, and that that is the principle upon which any disarmament plan must be based?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I are not at issue on that at all. Of course confidence is important. If there is no confidence there will be no agreement. But I am speaking of proposals. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that Canada had proposals. I am not inquiring whether these proposals embody the six principles that were laid before the United Nations on April 24, 1952. I am asking whether or not these proposals are designed to create the very kind of confidence of which my hon. friend has spoken.
Then there is the discussion that is now going on at Geneva among the three nuclear powers. President Eisenhower said without any equivocation today that this particular conference has a bearing upon the outcome of the disarmament discussions that are about to begin. So it is important for us to know what is the position of the government in these matters. The Secretary of State for External Affairs the other day, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition, unhesitatingly acknowledged that the position of Canada with regard to the cessation of tests was that the government was in favour of a ban on tests without qualification. That is a statement of great importance. It will be interesting to see, because of the position taken by the United States today, What the position of Canada will be when these discussions are ultimately projected in the committee room of the ten-power committee.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question, because he is being very helpful? Would he say what his view is as to whether or not that is the proper position for Canada to take?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition has clearly stated our position. Of course we believe unreservedly in disarmament. We believe that at this period there can be only one way to disarm, and that is by mutual understanding based on conditions of control that will give each side the firm confidence that there will be implementation of undertakings solemnly committed. That is a position which I would unhesitatingly take.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will now answer the question. Is your party against any further nuclear tests?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I take it that my hon. friend is as helpful in his question as the Prime Minister said I was in my comment. This is a matter that does not invite frivolity, and I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs would be the last man to be frivolous in a situation like this. Our position has been stated over and over again by one who is certainly one of the very few to have received international recognition for his work in trying to bring about a cessation of tests and in trying to bring about peace in the world.
We are not at odds on this basic principle. Of course we want to see tests banned, and we want to see them banned in such a way as not to give an advantage to any country that is prepared clandestinely to violate undertakings solemnly committed. That is the position this party takes, and I am sure that on reflection that is the position which hon. gentlemen opposite take. But I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in view of the statement of the President that these discussions in Geneva have relevancy in terms of the discussions of the ten-power committee, does Canada agree that there should not be any use of nuclear weapons in any kind of war? Does Canada agree that there should be no tests of new weapons in experimental research? Does Canada agree that there should not be any new fissionable or fusionable material made for war-like purposes? Does Canada agree that there should not be stockpiling of nuclear weapons, and that there should be conversion of existing stocks to peaceful uses at the dates and by the methods which a disarmament treaty might lay down?
In the British proposal will be found some of these principles. I ask, why could they not have been at least outlined in some general way by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; or does the government take
External Affairs
the position that these various facets of the banning of nuclear tests must all be taken together, that one cannot be accepted without the others? These are questions which I think the country and parliament are entitled to ask.
I believe a mistake was made by some of the western powers in unduly linking the solution of political questions to disarmament. I do not say, and I applied this in answer to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones), that we can fail to take into consideration the political controversies as between the great powers particularly. But does the government take the position that we cannot proceed, that we cannot have a comprehensive system of disarmament, in the absence of a solution of the major political problems of the day? Do we take the position, for instance, that there is no hope of making a real start on disarmament unless there is suspension of tests under adequate control, unless there is a major disengagement of conventional forces and armaments in Germany and her neighbours, unless there is an agreement regarding the status of West Berlin and some progress with regard to the German question? Is that our view? There was not a word about this from the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I am saying this only because I believe that in a matter of this sort, with a country like Canada that no longer, in the language of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is going to pursue the course of an honest broker, a country that is going to maintain an independent position, that is going to prosecute this question as it thinks it should be prosecuted, we have a right to expect more from my genial friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs than we got yesterday from his tour around the world that did not last 80 days but only about 90 minutes.
In conclusion I suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Canada should have a plan of its own. That may be a synthesis of other plans. The minister said yesterday that Canada has such a plan. I take it that it will be a plan that will enable us to look at the whole problem in terms of what might emerge as a comprehensive treaty. Such a treaty, even if it were put forward as an objective apart from the difficulty there is in the absence of settlement of some political controversies, would have wide interest in this country and in the world. I am sure if the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada put forward at least in general terms, in general principles, the point of view of Canada with regard to this matter it would evoke in countries like India, Indonesia, Malaya, Indo-China, Cambodia and the countries he spoke of yesterday a great deal of

External Affairs
interest. It would reveal to these nations that there are countries determined to try and do something about this problem. However, I regret that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not take advantage of this particular debate to do so.
I suggest that at this time Canada might work toward bringing about some agreement with regard to weapons not now in existence. We tried to do that with regard to the
I.C.B.M., and that was a gigantic problem to face. I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that with all the sincerity he possesses, with all the honour and integrity of character he possesses, he could play a great role in trying to impress upon all the powers concerned that if we cannot get an agreement on disarmament generally, might we not at least, in addition to agreement on the cessation of tests, get agreement with regard to some of these vehicles and instruments of war not yet fully created. Could we not urge the elimination of vehicles that might carry atomic weapons, such as satellites, rockets, supersonic aircraft, ocean-going submarines and launching pads that are capable of adding to human destruction way beyond the fancy and imagination of man?
There are ways by which this could be done. We could suggest a first stage of getting the nations to report their existing weapons and programs to an international disarmament commission. There could be a second stage when prior notice would be given, and when there would be some control of tests. There could be another procedure devised for the destruction and control of stockpiles. These are suggestions that come to one's mind. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I say there are many problems that the nations of the world have to face today. I believe the Prime Minister was right when he said at the general assembly of the United Nations that this is the foremost problem of all. Wars are not necessarily caused by arms but, as Mr. Churchill said in 1912 and in 1936, the existence of these tremendous weapons in itself is a potential danger to peace among the nations.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has declared that Canada's role is now to be one of independence, and not that of honest broker. During the past decade, as I emphasized yesterday, Canada has emerged as a nation whose spokesmen in the councils of the nations, notably the Leader of the Opposition, have responsibly and unhesitatingly put forward proposals which reflect our initiative, our maturity, our sense of responsibility and independence.
The government now, in this matter of disarmament, has the opportunity of making

the minister's proud boast a reality. It is not too late, on the eve of a new chapter in the discussions on disarmament, for Canada to once again seize the initiative through constructive proposals designed to remove the unbelievably hideous weapons of human destruction which, by their very existence, threaten the peace of mankind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member, is he suggesting that Canada's initiative in this regard should be taken in the way of propaganda, that is by announcing a plan to the world today; or should it be taken in the councils of the countries with which she is now associated and later in the meeting of the 10-member committee? It comes down to a question of whether it is to be a case of propaganda or whether we are really going to try to work out a sound, worth-while scheme.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs recognizes that the formulation of policy in this country in foreign affairs is not for the purpose of propaganda; that is the first thing. But having devised a policy there is a legitimate propaganda value to a very clear enunciation of principles and a plan, which does not in any way preclude the kind of private diplomacy which my hon. friend has in mind and which is, of course, essential.
I was simply referring to the kind of thing Mr. Selwyn Lloyd did in the United Nations, and that Canada has not done. Mr. Selwyn Lloyd outlined a plan that could be integrated into other plans that have been proposed. However, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, in proposing that plan, did not do so merely for the sake of propaganda. If that was a result it was a happy result, but it was not the purpose. Nor did he preclude the right, in private meetings, to spell out this plan with its details and its principles. All I am saying is that Canada has not done as much.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that Canada, Italy, France and the United States should rush out now with their four different plans for disarmament? Does he not realize that at the United Nations there was only Selwyn Lloyd's statement and the statement of Premier Khrushchev? It never was the intention that the whole 10 nations of the disarmament committee should rush out with 10 statements about what they thought should be done to bring about disarmament.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend said yesterday we were no longer going to act as the honest broker, we were going to act independently. Now my hon. friend is taking a different position; we must get the

consent of other countries. All I am saying is this. If it was proper for the United Kingdom to give a plan, as Selwyn Lloyd did in the assembly, and if it was proper for other countries to do so during the discussions- I have read them all-it was no less possible, and I believe it would have been equally timely, for a country like Canada that professes it speak not only for itself but for the other smaller nations of the world to have done likewise.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In
this two-day discussion on external affairs, Mr. Speaker, it is the right of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the hon. member for Essex East to have unlimited time. Being the third speaker in this discussion my own time is limited; therefore I hope hon. members will understand why it is impossible for me to comment on the eight points discussed yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or to go into too much detail on the matters which I desire to draw to the attention of the house.
It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that an eastern monarch once charged his wise men to invent him a sentence which would be ever in view and which would be true and appropriate at all times and in all situations. His wise men presented him with these words: "And this too shall pass away." Those words came to my recollection when the minister was speaking yesterday afternoon; and this too shall pass away. I was reminded of this because the minister, in his opening remarks and throughout his speech, made it obvious that in his opinion the old approach of Canada to external affairs had to pass away and a new one was required.
The main theme of the minister's speech yesterday was that Canada had to leave the old role of mediator and broker, and establish a procedure of independent, active policies in international affairs. We in this party welcome the minister's pronouncement of a policy based on independent, active participation. We honour him for that statement-and especially do I honour him because the minister comes from the same city as I-and endorse the principle. But in so doing I want to point out that words must be backed up by acts. Having been so greatly enthused over the principles and the motives behind the minister's speech, it was with a great deal of regret that we found that in the course of his speech he backtracked on all independence of action, and in his statement made it clear that he wears the same blinkers that have been evident in Canadian foreign policy over many years.
The speech of the minister can be consolidated into views on disarmament, world 79951-0-61
External Affairs
co-operation, commonwealth understanding and peace. If my condensation of his views and principles is correct I think perhaps one of the first words I should say is this. Canada can aid the achievement of world peace and international co-operation by a militant, active leadership in rallying the middle and small nations of the world around dynamic and constructive proposals which will make it abundantly clear to the sparring giants of the world, namely the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R., that there are other countries in the United Nations and in the world which have no desire nor intention of being engulfed either in an economic cold war or in a fighting hot war, and which have no desire or intention of being the pawns or the stooges of the U.S.A. or the U.S.S.R. in their sparring and in their fighting.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that Canada can give that leadership, can rally the middle and the small countries of this world, and can exercise an influence and power of great magnitude in world affairs. It will take courage and it will take leadership, but it must be done.
To follow up that suggestion I have tried to give an answer to the question of what kind of leadership Canada should give. To some it may seem to be a platitudinous generalization but I have tried to put down in a few words what should be done.
We in this party believe that the foreign policy of Canada should be such as to give wholehearted support to the principles and purposes of the United Nations. In words that has been done in the past and is being done now, but in too many respects it is not being followed through by action by Canada in the United Nations or here at home. We believe that Canada should do more-by action, not just by words-in promoting understanding and support of the principles of equal rights and self-determination of peoples. We believe that Canada should give greater leadership in proposing policies to achieve peace through negotiation. It is true that we have always supported that objective, but we can do more by way of active leadership.
We believe that Canada should show a greater interest in the problems and the aspirations of the Afro-Asian countries. Canada has done a great deal there, but I do not think the government is yet fully cognizant of the importance of the Afro-Asian countries and of what is taking place at the present time.
We think it is important that Canada should give a real lead in disarmament and should wage a militant campaign in order to gather support behind the proposition that

External Affairs
all armed forces, if we are to have them, shall come under the control of the United Nations.
As I said before, those suggestions may seem rather general, but if those principles are backed up in the foreign affairs policies of this country under the direction of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it is my personal belief and that of the C.C.F. party that Canada can perhaps do more than any other country or people for the maintenance of world peace, for the development of undeveloped countries and for prosperity for all peoples and all countries.
Naturally I will be asked why I feel that the magnificent words and principles expressed yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs are, unfortunately, to some extent only window dressing, and that the courage is not there to back up the principles which he espoused. I think the answer is quite obvious. There are still too many blinkers over the eyes of the minister. In his mind he knows what is correct, but he cannot see his way clear to put the principles into operation.
Let us take by way of example, two, three or four indications that bear out that statement. Yesterday the minister told us how the Canadian delegation abstained from voting on the apartheid issue before the United Nations. I know the thinking of the minister, the Prime Minister and the government. They do not believe in discrimination on the basis of race, sex, colour or creed. They do not believe in nor do they support the principle of apartheid as it is applied in South Africa. But as we were told yesterday by the minister, because of their love of the commonwealth and because, as he pointed out, of the history of South Africa and the commonwealth, they were not going to do anything to endanger South Africa's position in the commonwealth. They were not going to do anything to endanger South Africa within the commonwealth. I can understand that from the commonwealth point of view. But South Africa is not the commonwealth, and this is a matter of principle; and I want to ask through you, Mr. Speaker, if the stand taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), because of this membership of the commonwealth, is not going to lead to a position where the commonwealth is actually endangered, although the Secretary of State and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), too, are absolutely against what is happening in South Africa.
Was any thought given to the other parts of the commonwealth, especially to the Afro-Asian countries and those growing nations now coming out of the cocoon of colonialism

and which are going to be major powers, if not the major powers in years to come and whose relations with Canada will mean so much to us. Was any thought given to that when, in the United Nations, the Canadian delegation abstained from voting on a matter of principle; was any thought given to the non-white members of the commonwealth, the self-governing countries of India, Pakistan, Malaya, Ghana and Ceylon. What thought was given to those nations in the British commonwealth which are developing toward self-government, Singapore, the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, and the West Indies, or those nations which are progressing toward self-government within the commonwealth, the colonies and protectorates of Kenya, Nigeria, Basutoland, Aden, Bechu-analand, Tanganyika, Somaliland, Uganda, South-West Africa, New Guinea, North Borneo, Sierra Leone, Gambia, Hong Kong, Zanzibar, and British Guiana. These, too, are the British commonwealth and these countries, too, have one great interest, and that is the relationship of the white people and of Canada to the problem of apartheid.
You know, Mr. Speaker, during the meetings of the commonwealth parliamentary association in Australia one of the big discussions among the 48 parliaments of the commonwealth Australia represented there was the policy of discrimination in South Africa against the native population. These non-white nations are also of the commonwealth; they are a growing power in the commonwealth and if the minister means what he says by independence, activity and courage, then Canada will not abstain from voting on a principle. Instead, we will give Canadian leadership to those people both inside the commonwealth and outside it to show that Christianity and non-discrimination mean something to us.
The minister spoke at length on disarmament. I wish I had the time and the opportunity to speak at great length on that subject myself because it is one of the greatest problems which is facing this country today. We are very grateful for the interest which has been taken in this matter by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We are very proud that Canada is to be represented as one of the 10 powers represented on the disarmament committee. We sincerely hope that all the wishes of the minister will come true.
But, Mr. Speaker-you know I do not like saying things like this, because I know what is in the heart of the hon. gentleman-he is making it impossible to obtain the very objective he wants by the stand he is taking. Hon. gentlemen opposite want world disarmament, and so do we in this party. We are the only

party which has been fighting for this continuously, in provincial legislatures, in the House of Commons and on the platform. We want results. The minister says he wants results, yet after telling us for a long time about this 10-power committee and what it is going to do, he tells us, reading from a prepared statement, about the stand which the government is adopting regarding the People's Republic of China.
Mr. Speaker, we know of the arguments used in the past, and the arguments used at the present time as to why there should not be recognition of the People's Republic of China. But it is leading the people down the garden path to talk about world disarmament and then to stand up, as the minister did yesterday afternoon, and say that the People's Republic of China will not be recognized diplomatically, in the United Nations, or represented on the disarmament committee.
There are 650 million people in this one country, and whether we like their government or whether we do not, they are advancing rapidly both industrially and scientifically. How can one discuss world disarmament and leave a country of 650 million people completely out in the cold, without representation on the committee. Why the blinkers? It is absolute, plain, unadulterated stupidity for this government to be-I know the words I want, and I will get it in a minute-the ventriloquist's dummy of United States foreign policy.
Formosa and Chiang Kai-shek in the United Nations are not China. Why should Canada follow a policy which could endanger the peace of the world and the prospects of world disarmament by following Chiang Kai-shek on Formosa and minding about Matsu and Quemoy surpasses all comprehension. The day will have to come when the People's Republic of China, irrespective of its government, will be recognized as it is entitled to be recognized. The day will come when it will be given its seat in the United Nations and take its proper place in the disarmament discussions. Any talk of international peace, cooperation and disarmament based on the assumption that China is Chiang Kai-shek is just nonsensical. If the foreign minister was not my friend and if he was not in the government I would be tempted to say that there are people not so crazy in a lunatic asylum. What can we make of the statements made by the minister? I listened to his speech yesterday afternoon. In my opinion it was the finest and most concise talk on international affairs that I have heard during the seven years I have been a member of this house. I have not yet met a person who disagrees with 79951-0-61i

that. But we want to help him to do the things he says he wants to do and we want to take those blinkers off his eyes.

It was stated and not challenged that there were more United Nations ration cards than there were Arab refugees. The minister shakes his head but I advise him to look up the record. If he does not agree about the ration cards he will have to agree that nothing has been done by the Arab countries to establish the refugees. They are still there in an unsettled' condition. The statement has been made by the leaders of the Arab countries that they are going to be kept there.
This is something I did find out with respect to those who have a rightful claim in Israel. The money is being placed in trust every month and just rests there awaiting a settlement. As the Middle East is the danger spot in the world today, why does not Canada take the lead in trying to straighten out the refugee situation?
I wish now to speak about Israel. Israel was established in 1948 under the aegis of the United Nations. It is a member of the United' Nations. From 1948 until now it has been in a tough spot. We have heard a great deal about how one little spark could trigger off a world war. I want to know why Canada has not and is not now giving leadership in that area?
On January 9, 1954 King Saud of Saudi Arabia called upon the Arab world to wage total war against Israel and to sacrifice 10 million Arab lives if necessary in order to destroy it. That statement was not made in the United Nations but other alarming statements have been made there. Do not forget that Israel was established under the aegis of the United Nations and is a member of that body. The United Nations is the place where we settle our differences through discussion and co-operation.
Let me draw attention to some of the statements that have been made in the United Nations as taken from the records of that body. At the thirteenth session of the general assembly Mr. Shukairy of Saudi Arabia said in a meeting of the special political committee on November 11, 1958:
-Arab nationalism was determined to sweep away from Arab soil all vestiges oi colonialism of any kind. The fortresses of the retreating imperialist forces were falling one by one. Zionism was no exception to the rule, and its collapse would be the signal for the return of the Palestine Arab refugees to their homes.
At the same time in the same speech he went on to say:
At one time a slogan was coined for circulation in the Middle East to the effect that Israel is there to stay. Nothing is so empty as this empty slogan. Israel is not there to stay and is not going to stay. The United Nations can help to bring about an orderly undoing of Israel, lest it should take place in a disorderly manner and cause confusion in the area.
fMr. Green.]
On October 30, 1959, he said:
Israel and disarmament in the Middle East are incompatible and there is no room for both.
Let us turn to a statement made by Mr. Azkoul of Lebanon at the eleventh session of the general assembly in a special political committee meeting on February 21, 1957:
Were Israel allowed to maintain its character of Zionist exclusivism, to pursue its policy of expansion and eviction and to resort to the force that such a character required, it would one day either be crushed by a greater force, or suffocated in the isolation it had created for itself.
Canada is a member of the United Nations. As a party to the establishment of Israel and as a member of the United Nations I cannot understand why Canada would not voice protest against statements like that which were made in the United Nations or its subcommittees to the effect that the Israelites will be driven into the sea even at the cost of 10 million Arab lives and that the whole of Israel will be wiped out. To my knowledge Canada has never raised one word of protest in the United Nations. Never to my knowledge-and I have checked and checked-did Canada rise and object, and say that this is not the way the United Nations operates, and this kind of thing is not going to be allowed in the United Nations. The point I am driving at is this.

It is because it does go unchallenged, because Canada has not the intestinal fortitude to challenge that kind of thing in the United Nations that the situation has developed. It is because countries like Canada have not had the intestinal fortitude to get up and challenge this sort of statement that we have the situation now where Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Iraq can go ahead and brag about the situation where we have to maintain 1,000 of our people on the Gaza strip, and where sporadic fighting is going on along the border. There are two million people in Israel because of the United Nations, people who have, in my opinion, done one of the most magnificent jobs in this world of changing a desert into agricultural land

and mountains into industry, and are now faced by 45 million people who say they are going to drive them into the sea.
My point is that this is where we have been lacking in Canada. I agree with free speech, but when we hear such things they should be challenged. This is where Canada can give leadership, in challenging this sort of issue. These are the situations where Canada can give real leadership. You cannot by abstaining from voting on apartheid because we do not want to hurt South Africa, forgetting what it means to so many other peoples and countries in the commonwealth nor by not challenging statements against U.N. principles.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we enjoyed-and I did in particular-the ideology and the expressions of the minister yesterday. Knowing him as I do, I hope that he will bring them into being. Knowing him as I do, I hope he will see to it that his officials throughout the world and in the United Nations have the stamina, have the courage, have the vision-I do not like that word too much now-to make Canada the rallying point, the spearhead of all the middle and the small countries, because I am absolutely convinced that if Canada does that with respect to its foreign policy, then in the days that lie ahead not only the people of this country but hundreds of millions in other countries will be able to say that Canada made a contribution which enabled the world to have a greater heritage because it passed through our hands.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset assure the house that in rising to speak briefly in this debate I have no intention of endeavouring to supplement or qualify in any way the address yesterday of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). Hon. members-and certainly those who may have read the speech or listened to it-will agree, as apparently the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) does-that it was one of the finest reviews of Canada's position in world affairs and our country's attitude toward those affairs that this house has ever heard.
Those of us who were privileged to go to New York and attend the recent sessions of the United Nations came away with three basic conclusions: first, the high level of leadership and contribution made by the minister and his parliamentary secretaries; second, the progress which had been made in a variety of items which came up and have come up each year as old chestnuts; third, the new and conciliatory attitude of the Soviet republic toward the west, so new
External Affairs
to those of us who perhaps have had only a fleeting glance at this rather unreal world of international politics.
Whatever has been said in this house in any attempt to discredit the work of the Secretary of State for External Affairs will not be accepted by the world at large, let alone the Canadian people, because the minister has established himself as one of the great international citizens, and I suggest it is hardly in the interest of the opposition members to adopt such an attitude. Surely logical, honest disagreement in a debate of this nature should not be replaced by picayune partisanship.
I wish to qualify some of the statements I have made by outlining the actual contribution of the delegation representing all political shades of opinion. It is, of course, well known that Canada introduced a successful resolution on radiation, one which undoubtedly will, from a humanitarian standpoint, provide tremendous benefits to all peoples of the world. The contribution which Canada made in reconciling differences in the election of the last member to the security council is equally well known in the halls of the United Nations and throughout the world. Here particular credit must go to the hon. member for Oxford, (Mr. Nesbitt) for his untiring effort to bring the two sides together which, to a substantial degree, made it possible for the security council to continue its work.
The Hungarian question may be regarded as one of the failures of the United Nations. Here again it was considered by the independent members vrho attended the session that Canada's approach was indeed one of the most constructive ones. History will of course record to the discredit of the delegates that we came away admittedly with no real solution. The information which has come to light since the Hungarian uprising makes one very suspicious that atrocities of a nature undreamed of before have been taking place.
Here was a situation where the appointed representative of the United Nations in the person of Sir Leslie Munroe was asked to make a review of the Hungarian situation and was refused entry into the country or cooperation in any other way. Thus a stalemate arose from the point of view of making any progress toward discouraging and preventing any further atrocities from taking place in that country. Canada made the point that if these statements were untrue surely it was in the best interests of Hungary to cooperate with the United Nations and its agencies by opening its doors and permitting free examination of the problem because if

External Affairs
they were being condemned improperly or incorrectly this was the best answer to these charges.
The debate has dealt in part with South Africa. The principal point made by the government was the concern, which I am sure is shared by most Canadians, for the position of this commonwealth country in the commonwealth. The attempt made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat to suggest that there was only one factor involved in any consideration of the problem is hardly in keeping with the true facts. Of course it is essential and important that we endeavour to encourage this country to continue as a free member of the commonwealth.
Let us look at the situation in which the debate occurred in the United Nations. First of all, the resolution at the general assembly was considerably stiffer than any resolution previously introduced in the United Nations. It is true that the year before Canada supported the rebuke which the assembly gave South Africa but during the intervening period no action had been taken to improve the situation and therefore there was no hope of correcting in any way the racial segregation that exists. It is equally true that the attitude of many countries long before any resolution was introduced indicated to me at least that they were not prompted entirely by a desire to alleviate racial discrimination in that country.
But most important, article II, subsection 7, of the charter of the United Nations states in very clear terms that the United Nations is not in any way permitted to interfere in the domestic affairs of a country. On the one hand, you have to judge the advantages of endeavouring to create an improvement in any situation where racial segregation exists and compare that, on the other hand, with the tried and proven provisions of the charter which has in most instances proved to be most satisfactory. I think the real answer lies in the fact that in the first two paragraphs of the resolution on apartheid Canada supported the contention of opposition to racial segregation. But our chief concern is how best can we keep this commonwealth member within our family of nations and at the some time how can we work with them so as to achieve their confidence and assist their government in correcting their own problem?
We will not gain anything merely by passing one resolution after another damning a situation for which no solution has been produced in past years whereas by retaining their confidence we can work with them and thus accomplish the objective which is of concern to this house and the people of the

world. We have heard very little from the official opposition on this subject. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) did a very fancy piece of footwork in his speech. Of course, the record of the former government in this respect is equally clear in that they took very much the same view that the Canadian delegation did in the past year.
I should like to say a few words now about disarmament, a major topic of this debate. It is well established that today there are about 21 million people under arms. We also know that over the past 14 years east and west have attempted to reach some basic agreement on disarmament. From various world powers we have had different suggestions as to an agreement for limited or complete disarmament but these suggestions are only a partial solution.
We have had statements by France and the United Kingdom indicating only in the most general terms the method by which they would like to achieve disarmament for the world. The hon. member for Essex East argues that our government, as a member of the 10-nation disarmament commission, should outline to parliament the proposals it intends to make at the disarmament meetings. I suggest this would be sheer folly at this time, for we might as well recognize that we are still in a poker game with our Russian friends. While we hope that their intentions and motivations are as admirable as they may seem, we still have every reason to be suspicious of their actions on the basis of their record in past disarmament talks. I suggest that the true motive behind the proposal of the Soviet union can only become clear when they meet with us over the negotiating table.
There is no indication in the Russian proposal now formulated as to how they propose to overcome the obstacles to agreement in the past which have frustrated us for five years in negotiating with them. Even with a real spirit of concession on both sides there are many difficult problems that will have to be overcome. As an example, there is the question of how nuclear weapons are to be eliminated having in mind that both sides recognize that there is no known way of preventing the secret diversion of nuclear fuel or the retention of stocks of nuclear equipment.
I suggest it is interesting to note the variation in the Russian proposals over the past years. On one occasion they suggested a series of five steps designed to provide complete disarmament. At that time they suggested a method to bring about the elimination of surprise attacks. It is interesting to note that in their most recent suggestion there is no reference at all to the method by

which such attacks could be eliminated. In the past the Russians have tried to obtain from the west some decision on disarmament in advance of any actual agreement while on the other hand they have balked at any suggestions involving a satisfactory solution whereby inspection could become a reality. I suggest they have taken great advantage of the opportunity for propaganda to try to persuade the nations of the world that the west is using the issue of control to prevent disarmament. On the one hand they have been careful not to offer any suggestions of their own while on the other hand they are now critical that we are hesitant about coming forward with a proposal which we insist must involve a complete inspection system.
I therefore make the point, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs did in his questions to the hon. member for Essex East, that it would be very ill-considered at this time to enter into discussions having made known a complete outline of our proposals for it would simply provide the Soviet union with the opportunity to enter into another propaganda tirade and thus create a completely unstable situation and prejudice what will undoubtedly be the most important conference the world has ever known so far as disarmament is concerned. I am certain the peoples of the free world welcome the spirit of the Russian proposal for complete disarmament. Their motive, however, can only be tested, I suggest, at the negotiating table.
We have heard from the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) his views on the questions and problems of the Middle East. I should like to just say a word to the house on this subject. No one underestimates the seriousness of the problems or their complexity which affect peace in this area. There can be no doubt that one of the important factors in establishing an area or an atmosphere of moderation is the hope for an eventual solution to the Palestine refugee situation. No one overlooks the fact that there are over one million of these unfortunate people still living on very meagre rations. I think Canadians can take some pride in the fact they are third largest contributor in the endeavour to provide some aid' in correcting the humanitarian problem through U.N.R.W.A. and I suggest they have also made many attempts through the logical organization, the United Nations, to correct the long term problem.
But having said that, Mr. Speaker, I think it is equally true that there is no purpose in this house or in the United Nations carrying on with recriminations as to why the situation has occurred. The fact of the matter is we have a problem, and it does exist. What
External Affairs
we propose to do about it and how we propose to maintain life for these people is the immediate problem before us. The hon. member for Vancouver East said the host countries, as an example, have not provided any assistance, have not co-operated and have not, in any way, attempted to permit these people to live or to exist in their respective countries. I think perhaps it might be worth while to take the time of the house to quote a report by Dr. Davis, the director of the United Nations relief for Palestine refugees. He said this:
-the host governments have borne a heavy burden-heavier than is generally realized. They have provided land, water and police protection for camps, as well as contributing materially towards the education of refugee youth. In addition, they have carried a burden, no less real or costly even though less tangible, in the form of the complex political and social problems that stem from the presence of refugees within their boundaries. In general, the host governments have borne these responsibilities and problems with courage and perseverance.
This is not a statement from any politician or any irresponsible citizen, but a man who has made a study of the problem and who is perhaps the best informed man to make a comment of this type from whom we have ever heard. I do not, for a moment, underestimate the magnitude of the Palestine refugee problem. From the standpoint of providing bare maintenance or an attempt to rehabilitate these people, the solution of the long and short term problems has only been attempted in the most limited form. We have made considerable headway through this United Nations agency in attempting to rehabilitate these people in many of the countries surrounding the Gaza strip and, as has been indicated by the director himself, we are now at least in a position where we are able to provide some hope or some help for them in the sense that they will be clothed and fed.
The government has indicated that this year they are prepared, as part of Canada's contribution, to make a further contribution of $500,000. It will be recalled that last year and the year before they also made a contribution of $1.5 million in the form of flour. In my own discussions with officials of UNRWA they have suggested to us that any increase or any replacement of the cash in terms of flour would, of course, be a satisfactory contribution. However, this is coupled with the hope that Canada can perhaps still increase its contribution in terms of flour. I leave with the government the thought that the $500,000 contribution, which still makes us one of the largest contributors to this problem, is an important contribution and a very real one. I would hope also that these people

External Affairs
are going to be able to receive further comfort in the realization we will be able to make a substantial contribution, as we have in past years, in the form of flour.
The importance of this is recognized in that the contribution of $1.5 million last year in the form of flour permitted the United States to make another $3.5 million contribution, and as a consequence the agency was able to meet its budget requirements. Because of the stipulation the United States must not, under any circumstances, contribute more than 70 per cent of the total amount, our contribution was all the more significant. In so far as the long term solution of the Palestine refugee problem is concerned, it would seem to me that the logical approach must again be made either through the Palestine conciliation commission, which would have to be reconstituted to examine the various aspects of this problem, or through a committee of the United Nations which could bring together the two factions in the hope that they could resolve their own problem. I do not believe any of us in this house doubt the fact that so long as a million people remain on the desert surrounding Israel they constitute a threat to world peace. Recent press statements, which indicate that the members of the united Arab league may attempt to form an army out of refugees, brings the seriousness of the problem into its real perspective. The long term solution is the responsibility of the United Nations and I suggest at the next assembly one of the two approaches which I have mentioned should be followed in the hope that the solution may be found.
I come to the last point I would make and that concerns our own delegation's work. I have mentioned already the contribution made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and have made references to his parliamentary secretary. I should not like to sit down without saying just a word about another group of people, one of the most dedicated groups of men I have ever had occasion to meet, the diplomatic secretarial staff who advised us at the U.N.O. They work longer hours than any other group of people I have ever met before. This year they have made a very great contribution to the delegation, as they have in previous years.
I feel there is another thing we can do to assist our delegation and that is to encourage more members of the House of Commons to join the delegation. Canada has taken the lead in this respect because most of the United Nations delegations are made up of diplomatic representatives, in many instances without any representatives from the various legislative bodies. We, as the house knows 
very well, have a happy combination of both. In addition to the parliamentary delegates, we have a number of parliamentary observers. It would be my hope, so that the house could be better informed on the work of the United Nations, that we could increase this number and that we could endeavour to put them to work, thus making them all part of the operation of the United Nations, and providing a well informed parliament.
I should like to close on one note. In speaking on external affairs it is difficult not to make a reference to our relationship with the United States. The house will recall that a year ago we had a variety of problems over which we were consulting our friends south of the border. There were two committees, one a cabinet committee and the second a parliamentary committee. Both of these bodies have met and from these discussions have come a far better understanding of the problems confronting us.
Today Canada enjoys a better relationship with the United States, I suggest, than at any other time in our history. Credit for a large part of this success, and the contribution that has come from it, must go first of all to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to the government for instituting those two important committees and for the work which they have accomplished.
If you itemize the list you will include the integration of our defences; the establishment of a better understanding with regard to the development of our resources, with the Americans for their part showing an understanding of the need to co-operate with Canada with regard to the investment of capital; the sharing of defence contracts and so on down the list. I believe that Canadians and Americans today are working in more areas for the preservation of peace and for the development of the two countries and I believe that we can continue to expect from them the same understanding that we are prepared to give them. All this, of course, has come under the leadership of the present administration.
I therefore say to my friends in the house that we have made a contribution not only at the negotiating desk of the United Nations but in all of the embassies throughout the world and have established a reputation as one of the countries that can be counted on most. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, we have no enemies. We have worked co-operatively with all countries. I believe that the future for this country is as a great power, not just a middle power but one which has a role to play as an independent nation, one that can effect

many of the reconciliations between countries and that we are yet on the threshold of making our greatest contribution.
Finally, if I may do so, I should like to say this. During these last few weeks when the delegations are preparing to go to the world disarmament meetings, we wish every success to our own General Burns. I sincerely hope -and I close on the same note as that on which I began-that we are not prepared to show our hand prematurely, that we will deal with the Russians recognizing that we will remain armed until such time as they show the true intent of their honest motive.
