Mr. Speaker, I want to open my contribution to this debate by expressing the appreciation of the members of this group of the manner in which, in matters of external affairs, the minister has treated us ever since he became the minister. We know that he will take our arguments as criticisms of the policy of his government rather than of the manner in which he has discharged his responsibilities. The minister has at all times given serious consideration to any representations we have made to his department. He has also on a considerable number of occasions gone out of his way to accommodate members of the opposition at international meetings and in Ottawa. I think he deserves from the opposition a tribute for what he has done.
We are also tremendously pleased to note that in his opening remarks, as recorded at page 929 of Hansard, the minister had this to say:
There has been a great deal to learn, and I am afraid I have only begun to scratch the surface as yet.
In international affairs, on such important matters as war or the preservation of peace, I believe that humbleness on the part of our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) will strike a very responsive chord in the hearts of the Canadian people. Humbleness together with honesty, sincerity and forthrightness in the defence of principles will take us many miles further than will the old philosophy of diplomacy taking one step forward and two steps back and in effect not exerting the influence that our nation might be able to exert. Here is where lies our basic quarrel with the policy of the government in international affairs.
I note that in ending his contribution the other day in opening a debate on his estimates the minister had this to say as reported at page 940 of Hansard:
External Affairs
Canada can play a vital part in world affairs today, perhaps just as vital a part as any other nation in the world.
I should like to underline that phrase "as any other nation in the world". He went on to say this:
These next ten years could be Canada's years in world affairs.
I believe the government fails to realize the potentialities that are available for Canadian influence as so ably expressed in the minister's own words at the conclusion of his contribution. The minister also placed on the record the resolution of the United Nations that the question of general and complete disarmament is the most important one facing the world today. If it is the most important one and if the next ten years may well be Canada's ten years in world affairs, that tenet applies, namely that Canada will have to play a leading role in the cause of world disarmament.
I should like again to express appreciation of the minister's clear desire for clarity. I feel that not too much progress is going to be made in the extremely difficult negotiations on disarmament unless there is a desire for clarity.
I want to say a few words on the subject of nuclear explosions. Canadians were delighted when in very forthright terms the minister, on the rostrum of the United Nations, made Canada's position very clear indeed when he said that Canada is unalterably- and I think that is the term he used-opposed to nuclear explosions occurring in the world. I am using my own words, and if I am doing the minister wrong I know he will correct me. I hope that Canadian efforts to investigate the effects of radiation are going to meet with success just as they met with the approval of other nations at the United Nations. As I said several years ago in this house, for all we know we may know, even though there is no war, radiation may be doing more harm to mankind than has been actually inflicted on mankind throughout the whole of the last horrible war. I think it is timely that every effort be made not only to prevent any further nuclear explosions but also to obtain the necessary information as to the possible effects of radiation on mankind.
We note with a great deal of satisfaction the continuation of the present armistice between the Soviet union, the United Kingdom and the United States of America in the matter of nuclear explosions. We regret that the government of France has decided to explode a nuclear bomb. There might be national reasons for reaching that decision. I do know that the United Nations expressed its apprehension and pleaded with the government of

External Affairs
France. I know that Canada endorsed a plea to the French government not to proceed.
This leads us to the problem of nuclear weapons, and I have not heard an equally clear announcement of the Canadian position on the desirability of the establishment of a non-nuclear club among the nations of the world. We feel that Canada should say: we are not at any time to become owners of, or supply storage for nuclear weapons, and we invite other nations to participate with us in a declaration that they also will follow such a policy. I have a special reason for making this plea at the present time when many Canadians are viewing with alarm the growing aggressiveness among some of the leading statesmen of western Europe. I believe I can understand this aggressiveness originating from a feeling that possibly the United States and to a lesser extent Canada have become more interested in what is referred to as continental defence, and that the western European nations may have to shoulder more of the burden than they have been doing in the years immediately following the last war.
I should like to underline the grave danger of the West German government ever being in possession of nuclear weapons before the unification of Germany has taken place. We have seen history repeat itself on so many occasions and we may well live long enough to see history repeat itself to the extent that if the West German government is given possession of nuclear weapons it may arrive at a state when it may be prepared to take steps to reunify Germany regardless of the opinions of the western allies. I think that danger is very great, and it is for that reason that Canada should use its influence to make a non-nuclear club encompass as many nations as possible and use every effort to keep nuclear weapons out of the hands of the people of West Germany, because the fires of hatred, the fires of revenge and of fear are very rapidly kindled in a people who by their nature feel very keenly.
If we are not willing to take the lead in forming a non-nuclear club, we might well unconsciously be forcing nations to take part in a nuclear weapons race even though they could ill afford the luxury. Nations which must devote all their energy and all their resources to the welfare of their people and, in many cases, to the very survival of the cause of democracy in their country should not be burdened with having to take part in a nuclear armament race.
On the subj ect of international disarmament I have to make what I consider a very serious complaint against the government of Canada. I believe everyone wishes for international disarmament. Canada is going to participate

in the work of the disarmament committee, and I think Canadians will insist that there should be, on the part of our delegation, at least, a determination to continue negotiations indefinitely if necessary, despite all the obstacles that may appear during the discussions. I believe that a welcome beginning might be made if the disarmament committee were able to agree on the initial limitation of armament expenditures by all nations, limiting them to the present dollar value of existing expenditures. If we could get all the countries of the world to agree that in their budgets for armament next year the number of dollars which would be spent would not exceed the number of dollars which were spent in 1960, I think this would be a welcome move in the right direction. An agreement of this kind might be easier to obtain than an agreement on the discarding of military strength, because nations will hesitate-some feel, for very good reasons-before risking any measure of disarmament. Thus I feel an initial proposal respecting an agreement not to increase armament expenditures would be welcomed by all peace-loving people in the world.
I hope that when we take part in the work of the disarmament committee we are going to be sincere. Only the other day I read the speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made to the United Nations in September, 1957. He went to great lengths to castigate the Soviet union for what he felt was lack of sincerity in its disarmament proposals at that time, and he called for sincerity. Then he announced on behalf of Canada-he used the words "on behalf of Canada" and "I speak for Canada" were his exact words-an offer which, if I interpret the speech correctly, was meant to test the sincerity of the Soviet government with regard to its proposals. The offer was for a mutual Arctic inspection plan. This is very important, because if we could obtain a mutual Arctic inspection plan there would be no need for armaments within the Arctic circle, since there is no use having hidden installations if a potential enemy knows of them and has the right to inspect those installations. Canadians would be saved millions of dollars if we could have a policy of disengagement in the Arctic circle. The Soviet people would be saved millions of dollars.
I am going to pass over how in my opinion the United States government complicated the Canadian intention as announced by the Prime Minister at that time. I have not the necessary time, and I know many other hon. members wish to participate. However, when the present minister was appointed to his office in July last year, I asked him what had happened to our Prime Minister's offer

of a mutual Arctic inspection plan, an offer which had been made, according to the press, in the Prime Minister's own words on the rostrum of the United Nations. I asked whether the plan had been forgotten or discarded; I asked the minister to look it up. Apparently he knew something about it, for he assured me in an immediate reply that the plan was still good

still open-and that it had not been put away in a filing cabinet and forgotten. The minister used the term "filing cabinet".
Then we had the visit to the United Nations of the Soviet leader, a most important visit in world history, and we all know about his offer of total and complete disarmament. Many Canadians wondered if it was a bona fide offer and entertained doubts as to its sincerity. The Russian leader also offered to give consideration to any moves in the field of disarmament which might eventually lead to total and complete disarmament. I was very pleased to note that our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was not asleep at the switch. He immediately repeated his offer to the Russian leader and gained publicity in all Canadian newspapers. He said in effect: If you are sincere, how about considering our Canadian offer for mutual inspection of the Arctic?
Once again the Prime Minister was given headlines in Canadian newspapers. You can well imagine how surprised, shocked and dismayed I was when I asked about this on orders of the day the other day and discovered that Canada has never even had the sincerity or courtesy to make an official offer to the Soviet government. There is an embassy only a mile or so away from this House of Commons and we have an ambassador in Moscow. The Prime Minister, the government or whoever would be responsible for sending such an offer has never had the courtesy to dictate this offer to a stenographer, have it typed out and delivered by security guard to the Soviet ambassador.

Mr. Speaker, all I can say
to that is that the Prime Minister has never yet said he has officially made the offer to the soviet government on behalf of Canada. He has never said, "Let the Canadian government and the Soviet government establish a bilateral mutual inspection." That was the impression given to the Canadian people in the newspapers. As I noted before, the plan was complicated by the interference of another government and the Canadian government did not abide by its original intention of making an offer to the soviet government for a bilateral inspection of the Arctic zone.
I listened to what the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said about world refugee year. I feel that the role we are playing is inadequate and unbecoming to a country as wealthy as Canada especially in the light of what much poorer countries are doing in this regard. I also regret that Canada's participation in it has all the earmarks of a continuation of the racial discrimination that has in my opinion always existed in our Immigration Act and its accompanying regulations.
Much has been said about international economic co-operation from the angle of world peace and I endorse that. However, I should like to put forward the proposal that Canada's participation in trading blocs throughout the world and in international economic co-operation even to the point of aid to underdeveloped countries should be greatly enhanced if for no other reason than our own selfish economic consideration because the Canadian economy is of such a nature that it can only receive benefits through any economic aid that is rendered.
We note from time to time that the Prime Minister announces the participation by Canada in the Colombo plan and the aid takes the form of wheat. I am sure this is of great assistance to the prairie provinces. I should like to propose that our contribution to international aid be extended to at least 1 per cent of our gross national product and that wheat be an example to be followed by many other items of Canadian production.
We in our group noted with a great deal of interest although not without surprise- we know how intelligent, highly educated and well-read the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is-what was said by the hon. member on a recent occasion. His speech in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne was rather unexpected coming from one in the Conservative ranks. We in our group welcome it most warmly. We feel he made a [Mr. Diefenbaker.l
real contribution when he pleaded with Canadians to consider that their own interests might in the long run best be served by supplying much more active aid to the efforts of the government of India to establish democracy there and to help the people of that country.
The minister comes from British Columbia. I would like to add to what the hon. member for Vancouver East had to say on the admission to the United Nations of China and diplomatic recognition of that country by Canada. It is of importance in the cause of world peace; it is important if we hope to accomplish anything of any significance in the field of disarmament. China, with its population of 650 million people, can, in the years to come-not now especially because of the state of poverty that still exists there- be a tremendous customer and trading partner of Canada. The earlier we get around to establishing normal trading relations with the government of China the better off we will foe in that regard.
I notice there have been such organizations as the Vancouver board of trade which have for a number of years now called on this government to give recognition to China in the interests of our own economic welfare.
I want to conclude by expressing my disgust at the attitude of the Prime Minister in regard to the problems that exist in the Union of South Africa. All I will do at this time is reiterate what was reported by the Canadian Press on February 1 from Toronto, namely the sentiments of Sir Francis Ifoiam, a member of Nigeria's legislative council, who was in Toronto on that day and who is reported to have said of our Prime Minister's position in regard to the Union of South Africa:
If he could not take a stand as a statesman, surely he could do so as a churchman.
I feel that if the choice is to retain the friendship of a few million whites in Africa, or the loss of friendship of hundreds of millions of coloured people in Africa, I for one would rather lose the friendship at this moment of the limited number of whites in order to ensure the continuing and deepening friendship of the hundreds of millions of coloured people on that continent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the satisfaction that was felt in British Columbia when the announcement was made that the international joint commission had reached agreement on the terms it would recommend to the government of Canada and the government of the United States for the international development of the resources of the Columbia river basin

has been greatly intensified by the realization that this week, today, the first talks between the two governments commenced.
The present government's determination to press negotiations to an early conclusion was taken at the very beginning of this government's life. The Prime Minister in 1957 expressed the policy of the Conservative party at that time, expressed a policy that sought to implement an agreement on 50-50 sharing of downstream benefits payable in power and a cash return to Canada on the flood control account. To have arrived in less than three years at the point where, within the international joint commission, general agreement on those terms has been achieved is a remarkable accomplishment when it is considered that negotiations on this matter were first referred to the international joint commission 15 years ago. For at least a decade it was difficult for people who lived in British Columbia, particularly those whose homes- as my riding is-lie within the Columbia basin, to believe that the governments of that period felt any great urgency in pressing forward to a satisfactory conclusion of those negotiations.
Perhaps it might be difficult for people in other parts of Canada to realize how important this is to our people, particularly in south central British Columbia. It is perhaps hard to realize the intensity of feeling which exists there and the devotion there is to this concept of the development of the Columbia river. I think it can only be compared with the intensive feeling felt in eastern Canada and in central Canada with respect to development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Perhaps it is not generally understood in Canada-although I suppose in time it will become more readily understood-that the development of the Columbia basin in total in both countries exceeds, or will exceed, the expenditure by several times the development within the St. Lawrence region. In British Columbia alone it is a vast development, a complex development that is likely to change the face of our country and transform the economy. Therefore, there can be nothing but satisfaction felt in those regions that have for so long looked forward, counted on, and for so long not achieved in realization that expectation.
It would be, I think, very remiss on my part, if I did not pay tribute to the devotion and the lifelong advocacy of this plan by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). He, of course, as hon. members know, is a native of the very heart of the Columbia country. He has known throughout his life what this development could mean to British Columbia, and what
External Affairs
vast returns could be accomplished for the people of British Columbia and for Canada generally if agreement could be reached that would lead to the exploitation of the potential of the river.
I think also we must pay tribute to a devoted Canadian who has placed Canada's interests first at all times in leading the negotiations within the international joint commission and in achieving the large measure of success which has been reached at this stage. I refer to the Canadian joint chairman, General A. G. L. McNaughton. For years he took a firm stand, and he has a firm understanding and knowledge of, and devotion to this whole concept. The devotion and knowledge which he has shown throughout those years will bring to Canada benefits which are only now faintly realized.
I think that the vindication, the justification of the government's policy is found in the international Columbia river engineering board report which was issued last year where, for the first time to my knowledge, a very clear review was given of what was involved and what Canada would derive from the development of the river. The first statement, and an unchallengeable statement, but which has been in certain quarters and at certain times in our history to some extent challenged, was that:
Further development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin is practicable and in the public interest from the points of view of the two governments.
It is on that basis that the policy of this government has been founded, and the justification lies in this report, the realization that:
It is physically and economically feasible to develop a system of power plants that will produce an average of more than 16 million kilowatts utilizing about 50 million acre-feet of storage.
It is a fine agreement; it is a vast program and it has now, we can reasonably believe, come to realization, and come to that realization because of the determination of the present administration in Canada that it should come to realization. There are many other significant points in this report of the engineering board but I think they are well known to hon. members. If they are not well known they will become so in the years to come.
But as this realization has developed in British Columbia that the Columbia river development is no longer a dream, no longer something that exists in a future which nobody can predict, there has also grown the realization that there may be difficulties. There are complexities and there are problems. Now the people find that they must accept the fact that perhaps in the course of a very short

External Affairs
time they are going to have to live with this development and it will be with them and around them. It will affect many aspects of their daily lives.
One problem that exists in the minds of very many people, particularly in the Arrow lakes valley and as far north as Revelstoke, concerns the discussion that has developed within British Columbia of high Arrow and low Arrow, the storage of water on the Arrow lakes. I would think, that it would be well if the people in that region were reminded of the statement which General McNaughton made to the external affairs committee in April of last year when he said:
I think this is a pretty serious consideration which has to be weighed very carefully by the people who will have the ultimate responsibility in these matters, which will be of course the government of British Columbia and to some extent the government at Ottawa as well.
A little further on in his evidence he stated:
From the very beginning it has been recognized by all concerned that the people who will determine whether or not a project is to be built are those in the governments of the localities concerned.
He also mentioned that there is an intermediate suggestion and had this to say:
There is the intermediate suggestion which has been worked out, which calls for a level of 1411. This would require a certain amount of diking around the southeasterly section of Castlegar but it appears that it might be worthy of consideration.
In other words, although concern is developing in part of British Columbia now about what must be faced if the development of the river comes about and what this may mean in disruption and dislocation of their daily lives, the fact is that they must also realize that this matter is of first concern not only to the government of Canada but to the government of British Columbia; that it is of first concern to governmental authorities that the rights and interests of the people who live within the Columbia basin should be protected at all times.
I think it should also be emphasized that in any project of the vastness of the Columbia development project the people must be prepared for changes in their lives, that the face of the country will be transformed to some extent and there will be adjustments that will have to be made both by individuals and by communities, but they will only be expected to make such adjustments if over the long term the benefits they will receive from the project will be far greater and they will have a more secure and prosperous future than they would have if these developments were not undertaken.
I believe, that the success of the program of relocating town sites, the orderly development of facilities along the St. Lawrence

seaway, and the acceptance of the people of that area of the adjustments they had to make are an indication that no government is ever going to enter carelessly or without proper consideration of all the aspects upon a program of this kind without first taking into account the best interests of the people most intimately concerned. There are many other factors in this program that might be discussed. Having in mind the size of the program and the fact that it involves so many complex problems requiring the closest of co-operation and consultation, not only between the governments of Canada and the United States but also the governments of Canada and British Columbia, I think there are bound to be times when there will be conflicts of opinion and when there will have to be negotiations based on the sincere conviction that the case of each authority involved is fair and reasonable.
But there is no problem involved in this whole development that is incapable of solution by negotiation, consideration and a genuine willingness on the part of all parties concerned to bring about the development of this vast power and storage complex on the Columbia. Finally, I think it must be said at this time, primarily for the benefit of the people who live in Okanagan-Revelstoke riding, who have such a close association with this project and whose interests are so closely concerned with any development that may come about-this applies elsewhere in British Columbia of course-that if there should be any delay or deviation from the swift forward movement toward the development of the Columbia river it is accurate and safe to say, I believe, that any such deviation or delay will not be caused by any action taken by the present government of Canada.
I should like to refer now for a moment to world refugee year and in particular to the program for the tubercular refugees who have been brought to Canada in the last few months. I spoke on this subject in the house on two occasions last year and I should like to repeat, as I did on the second occasion last year, my appreciation of the consideration that was given to this proposal by the government and my belief that this is one of the finest contributions that Canada has made within the sphere of international relations in many years.
I must also say that I note that the program has come under certain criticism. It has been criticized in some quarters because it is not enough and it has been criticized in other quarters because it is too much. To those who have suggested it is not enough I would say first of all that when this proposal was made last year and the matter was discussed it was looked upon as a possible

trial program that would give Canada an opportunity to discover how successfully it could bring to Canada 100 tubercular refugees and their families from the camps of Europe and restore them to health and to find out how successfully they could be integrated into the Canadian community.
In my own speeches on the subject I suggested an even smaller program than was undertaken. I did so without apology because I believe that we would be dealing most unfairly with these refugees, particularly in this category, if we were to enter into a very large and elaborate program, as has been suggested, without discovering first whether we could handle successfully a small trial program. I think it must also be recognized that the government of Canada has no sanatoria in which to place these people.
The program can only proceed with the cooperation of the provinces and it is a matter of profound regret to me that my own province, one of the richest in Canada, one of the best able to participate in the program, refused to do so. But I still feel that such a program must proceed carefully. We must find out if it can be handled successfully and if the majority of the Canadian people are prepared to support it. As for those who have objected to the program, I can only say that I regret that there should be even the smallest degree of such selfishness and lack of humanity existing in the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take
part in the debate I should like to begin, as other speakers on both sides of the house have, by paying my tribute to the minister who gave us yesterday his first full and formal statement on external affairs since he took over this department after the still lamented death of his predecessor who we still miss in this house. I acknowledge, and I do it with great pleasure, the way in which the minister has taken up the duties of his office, which must indeed have seemed at the beginning at least somewhat strange to him because they were not exactly parallel to the duties he had had before.
Acknowledging his sincerity and honesty of approach to international problems, I can only wish him success in every effort he makes, not only on behalf of the government but on behalf of parliament and the Canadian people to assist in the search for a solution to these difficult international problems that face this country and face all countries and which, if we do not find a solution for them, may have catastrophic consequences.
The minister, when he was on this side of the house, more than once intervened in the debates on foreign affairs. He criticized the
External Affairs
government of that day very strongly, and very sincerely, on the international policy pursued by that government with which he did not agree. I know that he would expect us on this side to discharge our duty in exactly the same way, and if we do not agree, and express our disagreement with him on the manner and method of the conduct of foreign policy, he will not mistake that-I am sure he will not-for any disagreement with the aims and objectives of foreign policy which, under his guidance and that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am sure are the same as those that have existed in the years gone by.
I should like also to join with him in the tribute he has paid to the members of the Department of External Affairs, a tribute which has been repeated by other members of the house. I refer to members of the Department of External Affairs both at home and abroad. Perhaps I am in as good a position as any member of the house to appreciate how well deserved is a tribute of that kind. I might even call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that there are two ex-members of that department sitting on the front benches of the opposition and perhaps one of them at times-naturally I am not referring to myself-looks back with some longing to the days when he worked for the Department of External Affairs.
When the minister spoke yesterday he voiced the hope that this would be a wide open, free swinging debate. But I am not at all sure, having listened to his speech and having read it again in Hansard, whether he gave us very much to swing at. I am not at all sure either, that this is meant as a compliment. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) paid great tribute to the minister this afternoon, but it seemed to me he modified his tribute somewhat by suggesting that the minister was speaking with blinkers on and he asked him to remove the blinkers. Perhaps there is some justification for that criticism and I hope to be able to examine what the minister said without the handicap of blinkers. In all truth there really was not very much in the minister's speech to swing at in this wide open, free swinging debate into which he suggested we should enter. He did not, in fact, give us a punching bag so much as a puffball to strike at, and you know what happens to a puffball when you strike at it.
His survey was a clear, amiable and somewhat academic, I thought in spots, discussion of some of the areas and aspects of international affairs without, as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has already pointed out, too much enlightenment as to Canada's policies on the matters and in the

External Affairs
areas which he touched upon. I, of course, will try to point out those omissions on the part of the minister and I shall take exception to one or two of the things he said, more in regard to his emphasis and procedures than objectives. I hope that in doing this I will not be accused of being picayune as the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) suggested this afternoon such criticism might be. I hope also that in pointing out some of the weaknesses of the minister's arguments as we see them on this side, weaknesses which we think arise out of his unduly satisfied picture as to the state of things as he finds them, we will not again be accused by hon. gentlemen opposite of being prophets of gloom or doom, the kind of stuff we hear so often from benches opposite when we do our duty by trying to expose weaknesses of government policy. These weaknesses of Canadian policy are not to be confused with the strength of Canada itself, because my hon. friends seem to find it difficult to realize there is still a distinction between Canada and the Canadian government.
There was one other thing that became clear as the minister spoke. After the two and a half or perhaps three years during which my hon. friends opposite have been responsible for government policy there does not appear to have been any fundamental change in policy on foreign affairs, in any important respect or indeed in any respect. I am naturally glad of that. I think it is a vindication of the purposes and objectives of Canadian foreign policy in recent years. As the minister himself said, Canada's position in the world in the pursuit of these policies has been and remains good. There was no talk by the minister, and I am very happy to acknowledge this, of the restoration of Canada's position in the world during the last two or three years.
Where I do take some issue with the minister, however, and I have already indicated this, is in what I feel is the too-optimistic interpretation which he gives to some contemporary developments. He indicated yesterday his views and they were characterized in the statement that everything is fine so far as Canada is concerned; that we have no enemies in the world, and I hope that is true. I think evidence can be brought to support it. I almost got the impression, as I listened to him speaking and as I read his statement today, that we were expected to take the position in this house there was hardly a cloud on the horizon, except perhaps a red one over China.

speech. Perhaps I missed something. However, the minister did suggest there may be difficulties over China, that there was a red cloud over China which may cause some trouble, especially in respect of disarmament, as it has already caused difficulty in respect of diplomatic recognition.

I should like him to satisfy himself at least, if he does not desire to explain to the house, how we can have as much hope as we should have for the success of these disarmament talks which are about to open in the 10-member commission when a powerful, new, emerging, industrial communist state, the government of which controls 675 million or 700 million people, will not be represented on this disarmament commission.
Oh, I know it will be said that if this commission is able to work out a disarmament agreement both sides, east and west are represented on it, the results of that agreement can toe submitted to the government of communist China and the government of communist China can then be brought into the agreement, as it must be brought in if disarmament is to work. But it is a very different thing to include a state of this kind in the negotiations from the beginning and to 'bring them along if you cannot find out from the beginning why you cannot bring them along. That is a very different thing than to work out your own agreement, then submit it to them afterwards and say to them, "Please sign this; Please accept this, we have agreed on it".

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition a question?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does he think that the steps which have been taken to arrange for the meeting of this 10-power disarmament committee should now be held up and that a new arrangement should toe made to invite communist China as a member of that disarmament committee?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, I did not say that. What I am suggesting is that when the negotiations for this committee began perhaps it would have been a good thing to have had communist China represented on the communist side so that she could be in on these negotiations from the beginning and we could find out from the beginning where she stands.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What does the Leader of the Opposition suggest should be done now?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suggest we go ahead and try to make this commission work and try to work out a disarmament agreement through the commission.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is what we hope to do.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
But I am pointing out to the minister, who yesterday gave us such a cheerful and comforting picture of international developments, that it is going to be more difficult to bring about a disarmament agreement which will mean something when we have not one of the most powerfully armed countries in the world in the negotiating body from the beginning. That is all I am pointing out. It is too late now to do anything about it, I admit; but I think it is a weakness in the mechanism that has been agreed on.
As for the other aspect, this cloud over our untroubled skies, namely non-recognition,-I refer to diplomatic non-recognition- I have no quarrel with the stand taken at the last assembly by the government on this matter. In view of the policy and attitude adopted by the government of Peking, in the six months before the assembly particularly, and with regard to the onslaught on Tibet and the threat to India, I think it was quite unrealistic to suggest that we could have supported or perhaps even discussed the entry of red China to the United Nations in those circumstances. But this situation points up the dilemma we are in.
We have not this government which exercises control over red China in a position where we can call her to account for her actions. We have not this government of red China in a position where we can bring her into international agencies and try to find out her policies from the beginning. But nevertheless we cannot accomplish what we want to do in the world without her agreement. As the minister himself will admit, in order to be effective disarmament must include the red Chinese army in some form or another.
As to the minister's other argument for not taking any action to bring her in at the present time or under present conditions, as she puts it, he makes quite a point of the fact that our Asian friends would be upset by any change in the position at this time. Our Asian friends, include some of the closest, Burma, Pakistan, Ceylon and Cambodia. They are all Asian countries that have already recognized red China. Of course there is also India. Hence we have a problem there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he thinks that Canada should recognize red China?
External Affairs

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have just said to the minister that in the circumstances as they existed at the United Nations assembly last September, October and November, I think the position taken by the Canadian delegation was the correct one. But I also suggest to the minister that this question is going to come up again and that conditions may not be the same as they were last time. This problem is one that is continually with us and it will have to be solved. It is for the government to make up its mind what kind of solution it should seek.
However, I also agreed with the minister when he said yesterday that whatever action is taken, whatever solution is found-and it must be done eventually-we in this country should not accept any arrangement which would turn over to a communist government in Peking the people of the island of Formosa. I certainly do not think that solution would be tolerable. Formosa and the people of Formosa are entitled to the same rights of self-determination as are other people in the world. I was glad to hear the minister emphasize the desirability of maintaining those rights for them in any approach to this particular problem.
Mr. Speaker, as I am about to embark upon another subject, perhaps you would permit me to call it six o'clock.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before the house takes recess-and perhaps the Leader of the Opposition could go on after the dinner hour-I should like to ask him this question. In his suggestion that Canada or others could somehow have invited red China to the disarmament conference now taking place is he implying indirectly that there should be recognition of red China or of its admission to the United Nations?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No; I am not. If the hon. member had listened to what I said he would have known that. In the first place, may I remind him that Canada had nothing to do with the formation of this commission. This commission was agreed on in Geneva by the foreign ministers of the great powers without reference at that time to the United Nations at all and without, I take it, reference to Canada. Diplomatic recognition is one thing, but the inclusion of red China in international committees where red China's agreement is necessary in implementing the work of those committees is something else. We accepted red China at Geneva and when we had to work out peace in Indo-China. She sat around the table with full rights with other delegations. I happened to be there. But we did not recognize her diplomatically by doing so, and nobody objected to the

External Affairs
procedure at the time. I suggest that perhaps the same procedure might be desirable at other international bodies.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was discussing some aspects of the problem which arises from either the recognition or the non-recognition diplomatically of the communist government of China, and I was trying to point out that a decision not to recognize this government diplomatically does not free us from what after all is a dilemma, because there are certain international problems in this world today which cannot be satisfactorily settled without the participation and agreement of that government in the settlement.
That is an unhappy fact of international existence at the present time. We recognize that fact. Even governments which do not recognize the government in question were obliged to take that fact into consideration when China was invited to take part in the Indo-China peace conference. I would suggest, as indeed is obvious, that we cannot reach a disarmament agreement, important, desirable and essential though that is, without the participation and agreement of the government of that country. Perhaps when the minister winds up the debate in the customary fashion he will deal with this and with other questions which have been brought up and, indeed, with some questions which I propose to bring up now.
The minister in his statement yesterday emphasized the desirability of independence as the basic requirement of Canadian foreign policy. It does not seem to me possible, in the circumstances of the present, to talk about independence without at the same time talking about interdependence. There is in fact no possibility of any member of a coalition or of an association of nations-and we are members of more than one-taking any independent action without relating that action to the interests of the coalition.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would not want to misquote what I said. I think if he would look at the record he would find that my suggestion was that Canada should take an independent approach to these problems.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to accept that. Canada should take an independent approach.

But the argument is the same. It is not possible for a member of this coalition to take an independent approach without relating that approach to the interest of the coalition as a whole of which it is a member. That means attempting to relate its independent approach to the approaches being made by other friendly members of the coalition. That is obvious. It is obvious in respect of nuclear tests; it is obvious in respect of disarmament; it is obvious in respect of the use and control of nuclear weapons. The minister said he was referring to an independent approach as being a requirement for Canadian foreign policy, and I am not quarrelling with that except to the extent that we can never take an independent approach in an interdependent world without relating that approach to the interest of the coalition of free states.
Last October, as quoted in the London Free Press the minister, in a brief statement in New York to a correspondent of that paper is reported to have said this:
Actually there is no partisanship in the conduct of foreign relations.
There has been in the past, as the minister is very well aware, and perhaps there will be in the future, though we all desire to keep it to a minimum. The report continues:
But it is only too obvious that we have adopted a more independent attitude towards our friends and neighbours across the border.
I shall have something to say about that.
We are coming of age and we are no longer a vassal of the powerful United States. In fact-
And this is the example he gave at that time to show how independent we were:
We are independent to the extent that in the United Nations deadlock over the battle between Turkey and Poland for a security council seat we have consistently voted for Poland while Britain and the United States are supporting Turkey. The balloting is secret, but it is common knowledge that the Canadian delegation sided with the candidate championed by soviet Russia.
Then the minister went on later in the same interview to add:
The Diefenbaker government-
Not the Canadian government, or Canada-
-is asserting itself with more force and independence than its Liberal predecessors.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Again, these are not statements made by me. These are words by a correspondent, and not a regular correspondent, either. They may be shown as having come from me, but they are his expressions.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would not have used them as the words of the minister if they were not quoted. I will send the quotation over to the hon. gentleman. The words appear in this edition of the London Free Press as

the words of the minister himself, with quotation marks around them. If they are not correct, I will, of course, accept the minister's word for it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask who the columnist is?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Stephen L. Debalta, United Nations correspondent of this paper in Washington. The dateline is New York.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Unfortunately, that correspondent is practically stone deaf.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know this correspondent has a disability in speaking, but this is the first time I ever heard he was stone deaf. I admit I have had in my day to adopt somewhat unusual procedures in order to disavow what I thought was wrongly attributed to me, but never before have I heard anyone in this house say that a report is not accurate because the correspondent is stone deaf. I suggest to the minister, who is new in his profession, that he should be very careful about giving interviews to stone deaf correspondents in New York.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Sometimes you cannot help these things.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Anyway this was the statement attributed to the minister and perhaps the hon. gentleman will allow me to continue. If it is not accurate, the minister can correct it. I am assisting the hon. gentleman by giving him the chance, after all these weeks, of correcting a report which is in quotations and attributed to him in a very reputable paper, not a paper which is unfriendly to the minister or to the government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: He is a columnist.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He goes on to report the minister as saying:
We feel that Canada is growing in stature by the hour as a world power, and this is exactly what we aim to be-a world power.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suggest we might be a little more modest than making it our ambition in the immediate future to become a world power.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If the minister thinks that we can become a world power shortly, he will find that we are going to be asked to undertake the obligations of a world power, and the obligations of a world power are not such, surely, that a country the size of Canada should be asked to undertake at the present time, I for one, as a Canadian, am quite
External Affairs
content with the obligations we have undertaken in the past and which we may be called upon to undertake in the future as a middle power.
The minister himself said with regard to Canada's obligations as a middle power-I had better quote him now from Hansard this time; and Hansard is not stone deaf. On page 931 of Hansard of yesterday's date the minister said:
But I do ask the hon. members of this house to consider whether Canada would not gain more respect in the years that lie ahead and exercise more influence if she forgot about this role of being a middle man or an honest broker.
I do not think there is anything humiliating or wrong-indeed I think there is a great deal to be admired-in the role of middle man or honest broker. When I have mentioned this expression before I have always added it is very easy to exaggerate the significance and importance of Canada as an interpreter or middle man, or whatever you wish to call it. Nevertheless there have been occasions in the last 10 or 15 years, and before that, when Canada by playing the role of honest broker- and I would suggest that Suez was one such occasion-has been able to make a contribution above and beyond that which could be made by a purely independent Canadian stand. A Canada with only independent approaches cannot make her most effective maximum contribution in international affairs. This she can do by attempting to be an independent but honest broker.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member had better get together with his friend the hon. member for Essex East who said the opposite this afternoon.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, he did not. I have a very good authority for the importance of that role for Canada because not once but many times no less a person than Sir Winston Churchill has made reference to it. Once when he spoke in this house he lauded the contribution that Canada made to international relations. I forget the words he used but I think on that occasion he called Canada a link pin and on another occasion he called it a link. He certainly felt that our role as a middle man and an honest broker was one we could play well and usefully in the future.
Apparently, we are now going to abandon this role of honest broker for one of a more independent approach. The minister has already given some examples of what he means by that. He has said, and I quote his words, that we should "act aggressively for disarmament." Of course we should. As my friend the hon. member for Essex East has said, we have acted for disarmament for many

External Affairs
years. We have discharged our duties in that vitally important field with credit to ourselves as Canadians and I hope we will continue to do so, but are we going to be able to make a maximum contribution in this field by stressing the independent character of our approach to the problem of disarmament?
I might have been more impressed with the minister's argument in this respect if he had put forward yesterday any detailed plans or programs which would characterize this independent approach. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) derided that argument and said how silly it would be in this game of poker for Canada to make her hand known at this time. Other members of this commission, the United Kingdom, the United States and France, although not having made their hands known in detail, at least have indicated the kind of plans and principles they hope to put forward and follow in these discussions. Perhaps that would have been a good thing for us to do.
There is one respect in which the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) have been very definite and extremely emphatic, perhaps underlining the importance of this new independent approach. They have stated that so far as the Canadian government is concerned it is opposed to nuclear tests. That represents a change of policy on the part of the government. If we are having that made absolutely clear on the eve of these discussions it will come as a change of policy. It will also represent a policy which certainly has not yet been adopted by the United Kingdom or the United States as we had evidenced today. I do not quarrel with this statement yet the government certainly willing to make its hand known in this respect. The government said: We are against nuclear tests. But when the Prime Minister spoke on the subject in this house laying down the policies of the government in respect of nuclear tests on August 22, 1958, as reported at page 3944 of Hansard, he said something else:
The house will recall that on several occasions since I became Prime Minister I have advocated the suspension of nuclear tests, but always providing there was adequate international control to ensure the observance of the undertakings made in that connection.
He said later in the same statement on the same page:
The conditions that the suspension agreement be extended year by year only if the inspection system is functioning effectively and progress continues to be made in the reaching of agreements on major substantive disarmament measures, are prudent foundations on which to build.
That was the policy of the government at that time. Apparently that policy has been changed on the eve of these talks and

while talks are going on in Geneva. The position now is that the tests should be stopped. There was no reference in the minister's statement to the necessity of international control and inspection as a condition for the suspension and stopping of nuclear tests.
The Prime Minister this afternoon asked what our policy was and what we had said on this matter. My friend the hon. member for Essex East replied to that question but I am glad to give the reply in somewhat more detail so that the house will know exactly where we stand as a party on this highly important question of the suspension of nuclear tests, a question which exemplifies both the possibilities and dangers of taking this independent approach apart from our friends and allies on the eve of international discussions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Leader of the Opposition what the policy of his party is on this question?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I just said to the minister that I would give that. I am about to read from a statement which I made in Vancouver because I thought he might be more impressed by a statement I made in Vancouver than by one I made any place else.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: As long as Vancouver was not impressed.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I said then and I repeat tonight:
X suggest our policy-
With regard to nuclear tests. I continue: -should include the following:
(1)	There will be no more nuclear tests on our side-
That is the western side. I suggest this is the policy we should promote. I continue: -for a period of time, say two years, even if the other side refuses to make the same commitment. At the end of the period-
Or whatever period was adopted by agreement on the western side. I continue:
-the prohibition can be re-examined in the light of what has happened.
That is, what has happened on the other side. I continue:
(2)	During this period-
That is, the period of suspension on our side, without conditions.
-we should make a supreme effort to agree with the other side on an international treaty for prohibiting all such tests in the future, with appropriate measures for international control and supervision.
I went on to say:
The Geneva conference has made some progress here but not enough.

(3)	We can take the lead at the United Nations in pressing for a solemn declaration by all member states-
This was on the eve of the assembly. I continue:
-that do not now possess atomic weapons that they will not in the future manufacture such weapons.
There is no difference between hon. members of the house on that. Then I added:
It is bad enough to have two, or three or even four powers with the capacity for total destruction of peoples. It would be infinitely worse if 15 or 20 or 30 nations, including some irresponsible dictatorships, had that capacity. And that will certainly happen unless something is done to stop it.
(4)	We in Canada must be given full information by the United States on the fall-out danger from the small tactical atomic weapons that are now being developed for use not against cities and peoples but against the armed forces of an aggressor.
That is the position we took then and that is the one we take now. I suggest that is clear and unequivocal.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Just about as clear as mud.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am sorry that the minister does not understand it.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I don't, either.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not so sorry about that because I am not so surprised.
The minister then went on to talk about NATO.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is that?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization. What he said about Canada's relationship to that organization is a very good illustration of the limitations and indeed the dangers of emphasizing this independent approach to questions as a member of a coalition. I agree, and indeed I said when I participated in the debate in this house a few weeks ago, that the time has come, having due regard to our obligations as a member of the coalition, to push suggestions for closer unity and more collective control inside that coalition. When I did that-and that is an independent approach-the Prime Minister intervened and asked, "What would you do if NATO would not accept those proposals??" You could ask that question of any government in the world that attempts to take an independent approach to any international problem.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It took two weeks to think that one out.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
You make an independent approach and the Prime Minister asks, "What would you do if you did not succeed?" Because it may not succeed, presumably you should not make the approach. Is that the new kind of foreign policy we are going to
External Affairs
have in this country? If they will not accept your proposals, drop them, then, before you make them.
The minister painted a very glowing picture of the work of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which was in harmony with the bright picture he painted of international affairs generally. He suggested-in fact, he more than suggested, he said-that there was really no danger of the organization breaking up and I certainly hope he is right in that regard. But it does not help to preserve the strength and the unity of an organization to remain blind to the dangers and the trends that are threatening the strength and unity of that organization. The minister himself, notwithstanding his optimistic observations of yesterday, must be a little worried about the organization because he said when he came back from Paris after the NATO council meeting, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of December 14 in a Canadian Press dispatch from Paris that the United States and Canada alone were meeting their obligations to NATO.
If that is the case, how can the minister then paint such an optimistic picture of the working of the NATO organization at this time, if Canada and the United States alone are meeting their obligations to this organization? When I talk about-and I have and I will continue to talk about-some of those dangerous developments that there are inside NATO that threaten the essential strength and unity of the organization, I am not a sole voice in the wilderness talking like this. Perhaps the minister has read the words of an authority who may impress him more than myself, namely the secretary general of NATO, who has no reason to be unrealistic or pessimistic about the organization of which he is the administrative head. He takes a very sound and sensible stand in regard to that organization. I quote from a speech made by Paul Henri Spaak in the December issue of the NATO "News Letter". This was a speech made to the Imperial Defence College in London. The secretary general of NATO said this, and I commend these words to the minister:
That NATO stands at the crossroads and that its effectiveness, and perhaps its very existence, depends upon its power of adaptation.
He went further than that, and I agree 100 per cent with what he said, on another occasion. This is a speech made by Mr. Spaak at the Atlantic treaty association meeting in Boston last autumn. He began this part of his speech by saying:
I must now take the plunge and speak of my worries and anxieties.

External Affairs
A little later he said this:
Can we still afford, nowadays, to maintain attitudes, however excellent, which are beginning to be outdated? We adopted them 10 years ago, and this is a fast moving world.
Then he summed up his speech as follows:
The concept of a military Atlantic alliance restricted to a specific geographical area, adequate in 1949, is therefore no longer so in 1958.
A common policy, probably of world wide scope, must be added, to it. And this must be done at once.
Another thing which should be done as quickly as possible is the organization of scientific co-operation, and even economic and social action should be harmonized.
In a word, the Atlantic alliance should become the Atlantic community.
Perhaps the minister will agree that in the face of that evidence there are some problems facing NATO, some very difficult problems, and that it is idle, and it does not help NATO to overlook them. I could quote a good many others. The minister talked about consultation. This is a continuing problem and is likely to remain so for some time. Perhaps this problem will only be solved-and the minister, when he winds up this debate, might comment on this-when the governments who are members of NATO convert the NATO council from a diplomatic into a political instrument and send the kind of representatives to the NATO council who will be able to talk directly on behalf of their governments and who will be able to assist in working out a common Atlantic foreign policy in the NATO council.
I agree with the minister when he said yesterday that there is no sign of any impending break-up. Of course, NATO is not going to break up but there are dangerous tendencies. There are difficulties that should be faced and solved or NATO will not have the strength and unity so essential in the days ahead. As Mr. Spaak has said, and a good many other people have said, NATO is not going to stand still. It goes forward, or it will go backward. Some of the attitudes to NATO of some of the governments in the last year-and I pointed this out in the house a few days ago-did give cause for some anxiety. I am thinking not only of Prance's attitude toward collective security. That is one difficulty; that is one problem, but it is not the only problem. However, it certainly is a problem and if it is not solved it is going to make it much more difficult for NATO to go forward.
The courageous, heroic head of the French state, Mr. de Gaulle, who has accomplished some big things for his country in recent weeks, had a book published last December called "Generals and Fighting Men". It is the third and final volume of his memoirs.

This book bears careful reading and indicates what the French policy may be in the years ahead. In this book Mr. de Gaulle talks about "the vast design I have formed for my country". This is his design for France, and any design for France by a man who is now guiding the destinies of France is certainly an important matter for Canada and other free countries. He said this:
To ensure for It (for France) security in western Europe by preventing a new Reich from threatening it again. To collaborate with west and east, if need be to contract the necessary alliances with one side or the other, without ever accepting any kind of dependence. To bring about a re-grouping, from the political, economic and strategic viewpoint, of the states touching on the Rhine, the Alps and the Pyrenees.
The final sentence in this excerpt is as follows:
To make this organization-
That is this European regrouping.
-into one of the three world powers and, if one day it proves necessary, the arbiter between the Anglo-Saxon and the Soviet camps.
I can understand how the leader of the French republic must feel about the policy and destiny of his own country in the difficult days ahead but I suggest that for France or for any other European or North American country there cannot be found a safe destiny in that kind of program and that the only safe course for us to follow is not to try to build up a group inside the Atlantic alliance which can act as an arbiter between east and west but to build up the Atlantic alliance into a much stronger and more cohesive organization than it is today. If France seeks and achieves more independence in the coalition other countries will seek and achieve perhaps more independence, and what then will happen to our organization?
The minister also talked yesterday in his speech about the commonwealth. I suggest to him that if we think about the commonwealth in the old sense as some kind of association of states under the umbrella of Westminster, if we long for the kind of administrative and political centralization which some people in this country and other countries in the commonwealth hoped for years ago, we will not be aware of the importance, or the possibilities of the commonwealth in I960. The only chance of making this commonwealth work, as we all hope it will work for the benefit of our own peoples and for the world, is to accept wholeheartedly the new concept of the commonwealth which includes in its members now a majority of Asian-African states, to accept it as a multiracial commonwealth, to accept it, as the minister mentioned yesterday, as a bridge between the east and west. In that sense

the commonwealth may have a great future ahead of it as a peace preserving and peace strengthening institution tout if we look at it in any other sense we will be making a great mistake.
A good many speakers in this debate have talked about the government's attitude toward apartheid and toward South Africa. I do not think anybody in this house, certainly nobody in this party, would wish to take any course of action which would drive South Africa out of the commonwealth, but we surely do not wish to see a course followed by South Africa which will drive four fifths of the people in the commonwealth outside the commonwealth. That is the problem, and I hope that we in this country, or the people of any other country of the commonwealth, will not be faced with the awful choice between these two courses, either keeping South Africa in or driving the Asian and African countries out.
Surely it must be of the policy of the government, as of other governments in the commonwealth, somehow to avoid the necessity of that choice, but if we think of the commonwealth in old terms as a commonwealth based on London with white supremacy we may find that we are faced with some insoluble problems in the years ahead.

speechtext: No. I am not suggesting that the minister made any such suggestion. I have pointed out another dilemma, another difficulty, another problem in the international scene which affects the commonwealth.
