speechtext: We know that.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Someone says, "We know that". But there was one reference in the minister's speech which I think indicated a misconception of the nature of the new commonwealth. I refer to page 934, the bottom of the second column, where the minister said:
This commonwealth of ours is so spread out around the world that it must work for peace. If there should be war the commonwealth would be in far more trouble than the United States or the Soviet union because, as I say, it is so scattered across the globe, and certainly everyone in the commonwealth at the present time is working for peace.
Of course they are but the suggestion that if there were a war the commonwealth would be in a more vulnerable position because it is stretched out around the world, more vulnerable than the United States or the Soviet union, does not seem to me to be a very realistic one because it assumes that if there were a war every member of the commonwealth would be equally affected or that every
External Affairs
member of the commonwealth would be participating in that war. As we know-especially the new commonwealth with the Asian and African states know-every single member of the commonwealth has its own independent foreign and defence policy and is not under any commitment to enter into any conflict merely because other countries of the commonwealth are involved. This hangover, if I may call it that, of the old concept of a centralized commonwealth is not a very realistic one.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am afraid I am not the one who has got the hangover.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I just gave the quotation as an indication of the minister's own view that if there were a war all members of the commonwealth would be involved and therefore because they are scattered all over the world they would be more vulnerable than the United States and the Soviet union, which does not seem to me to be a very realistic idea.
The minister went on to talk about our relations with the United States, and perhaps it would be desirable for a few minutes to look at how our independent approach is working in this vital relationship, this vital aspect of our foreign policy. The minister had very little to say about this. I think he only had about two columns in his speech on our relations with the United States of America. In that part of his statement he certainly gave no indication that he was worried about the growth of continentalism as an aspect of Canadian policy, about the diminution of our freedom of action because of the growth of these continental requirements in finance, in investment, in trade, in energy, in defence policy, indeed, in almost every aspect including the cultural aspect of our national development.
When we were in office, Mr. Speaker, we knew about the difficulties of this development. We knew how hard it was to stand up against this trend. We were pilloried by hon. gentlemen opposite because we were not able to do more about it, and if we look with some suspicion on some of their attitudes and policies now it is because we remember that they were going to save the country from this kind of subservience. We knew the situation, we knew the difficulties. They did not. They were going to save us from the domineering influence of the United States. They should listen to some of the speeches that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) is making these days.
Let us see where we are in 1960 in respect of these measures. As I have said, the minister had very few words on this subject. He said that our relations are important. They are.

External Affairs
He said that our relations are excellent and that they could not be better. He talked about the Camp David hospitality and how wonderful it is to get around the table with your American opposite numbers and try to work out these problems in a spirit of frank and friendly conversation and, of course, we know all about that. You know, in other days we have had our Camp David conversations too. But the atmosphere of Camp David or the atmosphere of Geneva or the atmosphere of any other place is not enough to solve difficult bilateral problems. So the minister might have told us, and perhaps he will tell us when he winds up the debate, something about current problems and difficulties in the development of what I might call the continental aspects of our policy.
In his feeling that everything was all right, and this was echoed by one or more of his supporters this afternoon, he said-I do not want to be unfair to him-he gave the impression that we were really handling these matters well. We were working out our difficulties. Indeed, I think the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) said that relations had never been as excellent as they are today and that the problems had all been more or less satisfactorily settled.
Let me mention one that has not been settled, and that is the problem of our growing trade dependence on the United States, our growing financial dependence on the United States. This problem is more acute, more dangerous and more important than it was three years ago. If the minister and members of the government have been so successful in their negotiations with the United States on these matters of trade, economics, agriculture and all the rest, I wonder whether later the minister would explain why they were not able to make any headway of any kind in persuading the United States to carry out its announced policy of defence integration to the extent of extending our contracts for an essential defence product, which is uranium.
We talk about the necessity for continental defence. We say national defence is not enough for our country, and that is true. We say that we must integrate our defence tactics, our defence strategy, our defence equipment and our defence production. There is no more important part of defence production than the production of uranium. The United States itself includes uranium as a defence material in its statistics on imports. Some years ago when we were in office we made a contract with the government of the United States for uranium for five years. As the minister knows, there was included in that contract an option which the United

States could take up at the end of five years to continue the purchase of uranium. At that time, I remember well, it was a seller's market and there was great worry in the United States, especially in the Pentagon, that there would not be enough uranium for the essential work of manufacturing defensive nuclear weapons. The Canadian interests concerned were begged to proceed at all costs with all speed to produce this uranium as something essential for the defence of the western world.
At that time it looked as if we might require some of this uranium for others of our friends. We did not want to tie ourselves up indefinitely to a contract with the United States which would prevent us from developing that market in the other countries, especially in the United Kingdom. The United States said, give us first call on all your production for five years, and we agreed to do that. We did it to such an extent we had to get permission from the United States to divert some of that production to the United Kingdom. We were also assured that when the contract ended we would not need to worry about renewal, at least for some part of the amount. There was a gentleman's agreement. This was a matter of continental defence. The minister will recall that not once, but more than once, I told the government in this house that if they did not take this matter up with the United States on the highest political level this option would not be taken up; that if they treated this as an ordinary commercial matter we were in for trouble because shortly after the signature of this contract the United States government began to encourage the development of uranium resources in their own country.
Once that happened, and once uranium began to be produced in the United States, we were in danger. The only way we could have avoided the danger was by intervention on the highest political level with a view to making it clear to the United States that if defence integration meant anything at all, it meant the integration of defence production as well as defence strategy and tactics. An essential part of defence production is the production of uranium. I will ask the minister to tell us later whether or not this was taken up with the secretary of state or whether the Prime Minister took it up with the president himself. We know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce spent a day in Washington last April, but that is all we know. This was so important a diplomatic problem, and yet it was marked by the government's failure to do anything. If our cabinet ministers are on such excellent

terms with their opposite numbers in Washington, why were they not able to make a better arrangement in Washington, so that all we got was a stretch-out?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why didn't you sign tor 10 years?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman asking that question had been listening he would have known that I gave the answer before he asked the question. When that agreement was signed for five years there was a great shortage of uranium in the world and all the countries who wanted uranium knew it was in Canada; we were being besieged to make contracts with these countries. If we had at that time, under those conditions, when there was practically no uranium in the United States itself, committed our total production for a period longer than five years, what would have happened? What would have been the view of our friends? What would have been the view of the opposition of that day? When a contract was signed for five years, was there any voice raised in opposition at that time to say that it should have been for a longer time? No, there was not a voice. It was a very sensible contract to make at that time.
I am asking the minister, who has been telling us that our relations with Washington have been so good and that Canada's independent policy has been making an impression, why did we not make more of an impression on the United States government in respect of that particular matter. We failed, and I should like to know why we failed because I know what the consequences of our failure are at this time.
There is another indication of the difficulty of our relationships with the United States which the minister has not mentioned and which perhaps he will deal with later. I refer to the situation which was touched upon by one of the speakers this afternoon, our nuclear relationships in terms of weapons. I do not know what the position of the government now is with regard to the acceptance or use of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces, and I defy anyone who reads the record of this matter to be able to give any clear conclusions as to what the present position is. I mention this in a debate on foreign affairs because nothing could be much more important in our relationships with the United States than to get this matter cleared up. In an effort to do that, I asked a question of the Prime Minister the other day. I must confess his answer surprised me. Perhaps he will appreciate my surprise when I recount to him some of the earlier history of this particular problem as recorded in Hansard.
External Affairs
I do not know now and I do not think the country knows whether Canada is committed to use nuclear weapons from the United States for Canadian forces. I do not know whether Canada is committed to allowing the United States to have nuclear bases in Canada, yet this is as important a question in the relationships between the two countries as any that could be suggested. It seemed to be pretty clear on February 20, 1959 when the Prime Minister said as recorded at page 1223 of Hansard:
The government's decisions of last autumn to acquire Bomarc missiles for air defence and Lacrosse missiles for the Canadian army were based on the best expert advice available-
Then, he went on:
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads.
I think we had a right to conclude from that that the government had made a decision to use nuclear warheads on the Canadian weapons. If it means anything, it means that. The Prime Minister went on, on this same occasion, and in the same column of Hansard, to say:
We are confident that we shall be able to reach formal agreement with the United States on appropriate means to serve the common objective. It will of course be some time before these weapons will be available for use by Canadian forces.
He said, "It will be some time before they are available", which surely indicates a decision had been taken to use them when they were available. In the same debate, a little later, at page 1224, the Prime Minister had this to say:
Believing that the spread of nuclear weapons at the independent disposal of individual nations should be limited, we consider that it is expedient that ownership and custody of the nuclear warheads should remain with the United States.
This seemed to be a further stage of the elucidation of this matter, to the effect that not only would we receive nuclear weapons but that the nuclear warheads would remain under the ownership and custody of the United States. This was confirmed on March 10, 1959, page 1775 of Hansard, when the Prime Minister had this to say:
I indicated then that it would be some time before nuclear weapons would and indeed could be available for use by Canadian forces.
Then, on July 3 of last year, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) had this to say at page 5415 of Hansard:
I presume that eventually the Canadian forces will be equipped with atomic weapons under the same terms as the other NATO contingents under SACEUR which may also be equipped with atomic weapons.
The Minister of National Defence also reaffirmed that statement in November after

External Affairs
the Camp David talks to which my hon. friend referred yesterday. It seemed perfectly clear up to that time that we were committed to the use of nuclear weapons in the hands of Canadian forces under certain conditions which were not very clear.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why not?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Because they had not been made clear then nor has the position been made clear since. Only on February 9 of this year the Prime Minister had this to say, and I quote from page 867 of Hansard of this year:
As to the sharing of atomic energy information, it will be recalled that I tabled in the house on May 25 last year an agreement for co-operation with the United States on the uses of atomic energy for mutual defence purposes. This agreement was concerned principally with the conditions under which Canada can receive certain categories of restricted information and equipment-
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to note those words "and equipment".
-required by our armed forces. By means of this agreement we are now able to obtain all the information and equipment necessary to meet our immediate foreseeable requirements.
That statement seemed to be a little ambiguous for such a vitally important matter and so I asked the Prime Minister this question:
When he said-that we in Canada are now in receipt of everything that is necessary to meet immediately foreseeable requirements, was he referring to requirements in respect of nuclear weapons?
The Prime Minister replied as follows:
No; atomic energy for mutual defence purposes.
That was his reply, whatever it may mean. Are we or are we not-and the house and the country have a right to know this-as part of our relationship with the United States committed to the reception of atomic energy from the United States for Canadian forces in Canada or as part of our NATO contingent; and, if so, can we be told in clear and unequivocal language what are the conditions, if any, that have been laid down for such reception? I hope the minister who will be on his feet shortly will be able to tell us exactly what the answer is to that question.
These are just one or two of the problems in connection with our relationship with the United States. There are many others. But I want to give the minister the opportunity to answer all the questions that have been raised.
However, I could not sit down without saying something about our policy in and our relations with the United Nations. The minister, I think quite rightly, said yesterday that the United Nations organization-and

I am quoting his exact words-was a fundamental basis for the foreign policy of Canada, as it must perhaps remain the most important piece of machinery in the search for security and good relations between states. In so far as Canada can do anything at the United Nations and in so far as Canada takes any initiative at the United Nations-and she took some last December -which will result in helping to achieve that objective, the government will get 100 per cent support from this side.
But here again the minister must realize, as I am sure he does-he has now had some experience at the United Nations assembly-that there are some terrific problems faced by that world organization. As I said the other day outside the house, it will not be long before we shall have something approaching 100 states as members of the United Nations. A great many of them will be Asian and African countries, weak economically, without experience politically but each with one vote in the United Nations assembly which will equal the vote of the U.S.A. or the U.S.S.R. To maintain the effectiveness of this organization in the face of that kind of situation is going to be extremely difficult indeed and it is a problem that we shall be obliged to face very shortly.
I have suggested that perhaps one way of doing this-something that may be required in the years ahead-is to convert the United Nations somewhat from the concept of its founders and to make the assembly, the unwieldy assembly-the majority perhaps of which would be composed of these Asian and African members because certainly no longer does the west dominate the assembly-to a general town meeting of the world which will represent the conscience of mankind, where every country big and small will have a chance to express itself. The assembly then can set up smaller organizations to deal with ad hoc topics like disarmament. Then somehow we might convert one of the existing agencies-the security council, if that can be done-into a somewhat larger organization where the new countries and new areas and new peoples of the world will have a greater and more effective voice.
All these are problems which are facing the government at the present time. When the minister looks at these problems and the problems of Israel and the Middle East as well as a host of others, I am sure he will feel that there is quite enough to keep him busy and that there is no justification whatever for any complacent or easy view that

international relations are fine and that we are on the eve of great progress for the things we all hope to achieve.
We will never achieve our objective of peace and international security by ignoring the difficulties. We may achieve it by facing these difficulties, nationally and internationally; by working with our friends; by making, if you like, independent approaches to a coalition policy, to a world policy, so that one day, before long when we have a debate on external affairs, not only will the minister of that day be able to talk about the rosy picture for the future but there will be more justification for that kind of talk than there is, unfortunately, in 1960.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot hope to cover all of the subjects referred to this evening by the hon. gentleman. Indeed I know the house is looking forward to hearing the minister answer the many questions that have been raised. It occurs to me at this time- and I offer the suggestion now because of the variety of subjects discussed and the many interesting speeches that have been made- that my hon. friend opposite might agree that this debate might be continued tomorrow to the end that the various questions that have been raised may receive further and complete consideration. After all, we have listened to several hours of debate and the discussion of a multiplicity of matters.
I appreciated the opening words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he expressed his good wishes to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). Then after a few preliminary remarks there was for some reason the same frustration that seems to gnaw at the heart of the Leader of the Opposition. It has taken possession of it even in international affairs. It is a peculiar situation. The Leader of the Opposition is a man who has had wide experience. But as soon as he comes to discuss the problems of our country in any way he seems to lose that sense of equilibrium and balance that once characterized him when in another position.
All of us are agreed that the problems are great. All of us look back over the years and think of what might have been. Each of us, as he said, has the same objective, namely the endeavour to bring about international conditions that will preserve and maintain the peace. Indeed, I go back to 1945 when, speaking in this house following the United Nations meeting when the treaty was before this house for ratification, my concluding words were these:
Peace is an ideal which cannot be achieved passively. It requires sacrifice. It requires the
External Affairs
subjugation of many national ambitions, and abridgement of national sovereignties: the united determination of people everywhere to assure greater approach to equality of opportunity everywhere in the world.
I found it difficult as I listened to the hon. gentleman to understand exactly what he has in mind. He has consistently advocated an independent course on the part of Canada consistent with responsibility. In one part of his speech he advocates an independent course. In another he advocates what I might call a subservient course. He speaks of Canada not as a great power or a great power to be. I cannot believe that he does not realize that things have changed in the last few years.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Prime Minister has, quite unwittingly, I think, misquoted what I said. I said "world power". The quotation was "world power".

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have never known anyone who so often finds in the light of retrospect that what he said was something he ought not to have said.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is what the minister said.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think Canadians as a whole realize this. We all ought to have a degree of pride about this, not that spirit of disparagement which seemed now and then to creep into the remarks of the hon. gentleman. There should be pride in the fact that Canada today is being visited by leaders of all mankind. I speak of the visit of the prime minister of the Netherlands, the president of Mexico, the prime minister of the Ivory Coast, the Crown Prince and Princess of Ethiopia, the foreign minister of Norway, the defence minister of Germany, the prime minister and the foreign minister of Japan; I speak, also, of the forthcoming visits by the prime minister and the foreign minister of Italy, and later on, by the president of France, to whom the Leader of the Opposition referred in most laudatory terms; a man who represents in the view of Canadians as a whole, a land dear to our hearts and which is today facing conditions which all of us hope will be resolved in a degree of achievement in that nation which will raise her to even greater glories than in the past.
In other words, we live in an age of international exchange. Consultations are taking place with regularity.
Mention was made by the Leader of the Opposition of NATO. In so far as NATO is concerned we took a very strong stand last year that NATO must expand and advance along the course of collaboration, consideration and discussion. We took a stand against anything in the nature of a triumvirate or a council of NATO determining the course

External Affairs
of NATO. In other words, our attitude has been one desirous of the fullest consultation, without which none of the nations of the free world can achieve that unity without which there is no survival.
The same applies to the commonwealth, and I am not going to say more than a word with regard to the commonwealth. I listened to what the hon. gentleman had to say, and with much of his words in this regard I was in agreement-the tremendous part that is played by the varying parts of this commonwealth, the emergence and development of the commonwealth concept, and so forth. I saw something of the beginnings of this commonwealth in February of 1917, I think it was, when at the opening of the British parliament in that year the troops which escorted the reigning monarch to the opening ceremony were all troops of the Boers in the years 1897 to 1900. That was the beginning of the concept initiated by Jan Christian Smuts, using the words of an earlier day-the words of Rosebery in 1890:
The word "commonwealth" which in the passing years has resulted in an evolutionary process which continues unabated.
Both hon. gentlemen, the minister and the Leader of the Opposition, spoke of the commonwealth as a bridge between east and west, and I believe that. I am of those who believe that one of the major elements necessary to assure the fullest co-operation between the varying parts of the commonwealth is not any centralized authority, but through the medium of such organizations as the prime ministers' conference, the next one of which will be convened early in May. I go further than that, and say this: my belief is that the commonwealth prime ministers conference should as far as practicable meet once a year to the end that in a few days of discussion, while no decisions are finally made determinations may be arrived at of benefit not only to the peoples of the commonwealth but for mankind itself.
When one thinks of the conference of 1957, one realizes that out of that conference came the convening of a trade and economic conference which took place in the city of Montreal in September of 1958. Out of that conference came a system of commonwealth scholarships which in my opinion represent one of the most effective courses of action to unite the various parts of the commonwealth and remove those causes of difficulty because of colour and of race from which all mankind has suffered in every generation.
While mention was made a few moments ago by the Leader of the Opposition of the trade situation between Canada and the United States, I would point out that on January 7 this year the president of the board

of trade of the United Kingdom, the Right Hon. Mr. Maudling, emphasized the importance of expanding trade between Canada and the United Kingdom and spoke with satisfaction of the increase of British sales in Canada, expressing the hope of an expanding trade both ways. In other words, out of that conference came certain practical benefits for the people of this commonwealth.
This evening I intend to deal particularly with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I thought he made a most effective contribution to the subject before us on this occasion. Before I do so, however, and while it will not make for order-and order never arises out of a debating speech-I want to refer for just a moment to almost the concluding remarks of the Leader of the Opposition when he referred to the uranium situation.
I have read what has been said-and the hon. gentleman has re-emphasized it-to the effect that this government was responsible in some way for what is called the failure to secure an extension beyond 1962 of the contracts made by the former government. I believe I can do no better than to quote some of the remarks recorded in Hansard at the time which indicate that the hon. gentleman, a member of the then government, must not have realized the fact that the contracts entered into for uranium would terminate in 1962, and that there was not any indication that following that date governments would underwrite in any way the cost or the purchase of uranium. Agreements were entered into. They were gentlemen's agreements. The government of that day knew that when 1962 came that would be the end, to all intents and purposes, of this large export to the United States. I turn to the words of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe as reported at page 6440 of Hansard of July 20, 1955:
I know of no present shortage of uranium. Our production goes up steadily-
Then these words:
The situation is that no government is prepared to underwrite the purchase of uranium produced after 1962.
They knew that. Mr. Howe made it very clear. He then went on to say as reported at page 6441 of the same date:
I believe there will be a peacetime market for uranium. At that time the government will not be underwriting purchases.
I ask you, sir, who is responsible for the situation today, unfortunate as it is? The government of which the present Leader of the Opposition was a member realized that

in the agreements entered into after 1962 the government would not be underwriting purchases.
I turn now to the words of Mr. Howe as reported at page 1740 of Hansard of March 2, 1956:
The bulk of the uranium under contract goes to the atomic energy commission of the United States. When the contracts are completed, the contracts that are filed before the 31 March this year and approved by Canada and by the atomic energy commission we are informed that the foreseeable needs of the atomic energy commission of the United States for uranium from Canada will have been fulfilled.
Those three quotations from the words of Mr. Howe, the responsible minister, indicate that he knew that when 1962 came around those uranium contracts which provided so satisfactory an export would no longer be underwritten by governments. All that the last government did was to achieve some kind of an ephemeral gentlemen's agreement which said in effect that if everything goes all right everything will go all right with the export of uranium.
Now, the hon. member says, what did this government do? It made strong representations to the United States. In the intervening years not only has the demand for uranium gone down but indeed when one looks back over the years and examines the definition of uranium in the Encyclopedia Britannica, I believe in the 1920 edition, it is described as a valueless metal. Today we find ourselves in the position of having seen in the interventing years the United States engage in the production of its own uranium and demands for the metal are steadily decreasing.
When the Leader of the Opposition endeavours to pin responsibility on this government in that connection it is a case of the responsibility resting on him and his associates in the former administration for having failed to bring about when the contracts were entered into anything in the nature of a continuation after 1962.
What we did was this. Instead of having a cut-off date that would have put the uranium industry or a major portion of the business of this country out of business almost over night, we brought about a continuation of the contracts by a spread-over to the end that the sharpness of the termination of contracts would not bring about untoward sudden economic dislocation in the country.
I wish now to refer to the question of disarmament which was dealt with very thoroughly and completely by the hon. member for Essex East. He realized the difficulties of the problem. He realized the alterations in the perspective of mankind, the changes in a period of 15 years since the United Nations was founded, the discovery
External Affairs
and development of nuclear weapons, the tremendous power of emergent people all over the world to new sovereignties, the population explosion with its incalculable effects on this and succeeding generations, the scientific breakthrough and the ever-widening explorations of space. To meet this situation and these changing concepts new steps have to be taken. All of us search for an international institution that will resolve old and new conflicts, that will assure to mankind common security, welfare and international peace. These are no longer theoretical exercises of the mind, they are necessities for survival.
The hon. member for Essex East expressed the view that the government should place before parliament the representations it intends to make and has made regarding this problem of disarmament. The Leader of the Opposition says he does not want an independent course for Canada.

I do not know what these interruptions are. I listened to the hon. gentleman with patience, but he persists in those undertone interruptions, and I wish he would desist.
The hon. member for Essex East apparently believes that each nation should produce a collection of competing plans. What we believe is that there should be an agreed western position to serve as a point of departure in the negotiations with the U.S.S.R. in the 10-power talks which start next month in Geneva, and this is what we are aiming at: to make a contribution by the submission of proposals and comments which will assist in bringing about a plan for international disarmament which will be realistic, negotiable, and at the same time not imperil national security.
The hon. member for Essex East seemed to indicate that the United States was acting in such a way as not to assure that measure of agreement on this question which is the hope of mankind. Indeed, while he did not mention the United States in that connection when he spoke in Montreal on February 9 to the Canadian Club, he did say this, and I quote from the Montreal Star report:
Paul Martin outlines plan for disarmament.
Then, we find the following:
But Mr. Martin felt that the United States had also made a "great mistake" after the 1955 Geneva conference by being too adamant on its own program for disarmament and by tying in as well the settlement of political questions.
I agree with him that we should not join the settlement of political questions as such with the immediate problem of disarmament. I think that is of the essence, and that we should endeavour first by the ending of nuclear tests then by such measures of disarmament as are agreed to by stages to ensure that ultimately disarmament, the hope of mankind, will be attained.
Mention was made of the number of times that the question of disarmament has been discussed. The hon. gentleman went back to the days of Castlereagh, and he quoted from Sir Winston Churchill. I think one of the best epitomes of the whole problem of disarmament is to be found in the "Public Papers and Addresses" of Franklin D. Roosevelt, 1933. It is entitled, "An Appeal to the Nations of the World on the basis of disarmament and an end of economic chaos". Those words of 1933, which had the effect of mobilizing the thinking of mankind and the support of the nations, as evidenced by the replies that were made to this message did not, however, deny the outbreak of war six years later. These are some of the statements that the president made at that time. He said:

The disarmament conference has laboured for more than a year and, as yet, has been unable to reach satisfactory conclusions. Confused purposes still clash dangerously. Our duty lies in the direction of bringing practical results through concerted action based upon the greatest good to the greatest number. Before the imperative call of this great duty, petty obstacles must be swept away and petty aims forgotten. A selfish victory is always destined to be an ultimate defeat. The furtherance of durable peace for our generation in every part of the world is the only goal worthy of our best efforts.
Then, he sets out the plan and says:
If all nations will agree wholly to eliminate from possession and use the weapons which make possible a successful attack, defences automatically will become impregnable, and the frontiers and independence of every nation will become secure.
The ultimate objective of the disarmament conference must be the complete elimination of all offensive weapons. The immediate objective is a substantial reduction of some of these weapons and the elimination of many others.
You will remember, sir, the naval program of the 1920's, you will remember, sir, the Kellogg-Briand pact of 1926.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was 1928.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I recall very well when Mr. Mackenzie King, the then member for Prince Albert, came to Prince Albert for a couple of days and said he was on his way to Paris, and that in a few short days a pact would be signed there which would forever abolish war as an instrument for the settlement of disputes between the nations.
The Leader of the Opposition says that while peace is the aim and the purpose, we must not be fooled into believing that the events of recent months or years would lead us to expect that we are about to achieve that which mankind has tried for for generations. With these views I agree; none the less one must admit that in the last several months there has been an easing of tensions to such an extent that the hopes of mankind have been raised. The responsibility, therefore, on the part of those who have positions of international trust is the greater; for if we fail at this time, the potentialities for the future are certainly dark and grey.
While Mr. Khrushchev has been more conciliatory, he has also been most threatening. In the last speech he delivered in January, when he undertook to reduce the armed forces, he pointed out that they had an overwhelming supply of nuclear weapons. He used these words:
After the launching of soviet sputniks and rockets, the Americans have come to realize that the United States is no less vulnerable to attack than any other country.
Then, he went on to say:
The U.S.S.R. army has such arms as have heretofore been unknown to man.

Again, he said:
The U.S.S.R. has piled up such atomic and nuclear weapons and has powerful rocket equipment.
Then he promised the ultimate triumph, not by war but by economic destruction in the years ahead, for he said that the year 1959 was marked by success of the U.S.S.R. in the struggle for peace and the strengthening of the camp of socialism. He promised to reduce the numbers of men, but he ended up by saying that even when this is done his country will still be the most powerful in the world.
The hon. gentleman said that we should place before the House of Commons the actual representations that we have made or intend to make.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What I said was that we should place before parliament our concepts in the form in which, for instance, the United Kingdom presented theirs, in the open and public assembly of the United Nations.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I accept that correction. The hon. member says that we should give a general idea of the concepts, if I understand him aright. I could summarize them in this way. These are views expressed in summary which I think represent the thinking of Canadians as a whole on this matter. First, Canada's policy should be directed to the achievement of maximum disarmament and the reduction of armed forces which can be verified and controlled without endangering the security of the nation against aggression.
Second, whatever is done cannot be achieved overnight and will require to be done by steps or stages. To that end I suggest that immediate consideration and priority might be given to the control of missiles designed to deliver nuclear weapons of mass destruction and also to bring about an agreement whereby the location of missile sites should be designated.
Third, at the conference at Pugwash much was said regarding biological and chemical weapons. I believe the time has come that the nations should agree that the manufacture and use of biological and chemical weapons should be banned.
Fourth, we come to the problem which transcends all these problems, namely that of outer space. If we are to preserve the future of mankind I believe that outer space should now, before further advances are made in its exploration, be declared banned to other than peaceful purposes and that the mounting of armaments on satellites should be outlawed. These are several suggestions that I think represent initial steps, for if there
External Affairs
is any desire on the part of the nations to bring about disarmament those principles could be accepted and I think should be accepted.
Now then you say, what about the production of fissile material for weapons? I think that was one of the questions asked. I would think that a major course leading to disarmament would be a declaration that the production of fissile material for weapons should be ended and that existing stocks should be transferred to peaceful uses as soon as a practical plan can be agreed upon. You say, what about the interim? You proceed by stages. What will you do in the meantime? How do you preserve the security of your state?
That brings me to one further step, and it is not a new one. It has been advanced since the 1600's that an international military force should be begun whose capability would be the restraining of nations from aggression. I digress for a moment to answer a statement made this afternoon by one hon. member who was filled with remorse, horror and shock that the government had not placed before the U.S.S.R. its willingness to set aside the Arctic areas of Canada to mutual inspection provided a like right was granted by the U.S.S.R. I first direct the attention of the house to my remarks on August 22, 1958. I do not want to spend long on this but I have to point out the fact that on that occasion I said, as found at page 3944 of Hansard:
For our part I can give unqualified assurances that to the extent that the control arrangements which may be agreed upon might be applicable to Canadian territory, we are prepared to co-operate in setting up control stations and inspection of the kind outlined in the report of the experts.
Apparently this was not read or, if read, not understood.
Indeed, on more than one occasion Canada has agreed unreservedly to her northern areas and Arctic regions being made available for inspection in order to ensure that surprise attacks will not take place.
These views have been communicated to Mr. Khrushchev on two occasions. The first was on January 18, 1958 when I wrote him and said this:
I give assurance that in the context of a disarmament agreement the Canadian government would be willing to open all or part of Canada to aerial and ground inspection on a basis of reciprocity. It seems to me that this is the type of proposal which should prove attractive to both our countries since we are neighbours across the Arctic. I have in mind in particular the kind of proposal Canada joined in sponsoring last August involving a system of inspection in the Arctic regions. We were willing then and are willing now to take such action in order to provide assurance against the fear of surprise attack.
This was turned down by Mr. Khrushchev in a subsequent letter or at least he 'did not

External Affairs
deal with the matter because he said we would have to have it as part of a world agreement. On May 9, 1958, I wrote to him in part as follows:
If you are really anxious about developments in the Arctic and if you wish to eliminate the possibility of surprise attack across the polar regions, I And it hard to understand why you should cast aside a proposal designed to increase mutual security in that area. Let me repeat here, Mr. Chairman, that we stand by our offer to make available for international inspection or control any part of our territory, in exchange for a comparable concession on your part. I would hope that you would accept some arrangement along these lines not only as an indication of our good faith but as part of a first, experimental step in building a system of international safeguards against surprise attack. When there is, by your own admission, a danger of nuclear war breaking out by accident or miscalculation, it is difficult for Canadians to comprehend your refusal to engage even in technical discussions intended to explore the feasibility of an international system of control.
That was Canada's stand.

speechtext: I wonder-

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: My time is limited. I am answering the hon. gentleman now. That was Canada's stand. That is the stand which we took not only in the United Nations but subsequently under the circumstances to which I have referred.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not bilaterally.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I doubt whether the hon. gentleman knows what bilateral means. Going on from there, and I hasten to conclude, I think that if the nations really desire to bring about disarmament and peace there is one field that could constitute an initial step, a course alongside one or other of the courses to which I have referred, and that is the acceptance of the jurisdiction of an international court of justice, the predecessor of which was the permanent court of international justice. All through the years the stand that we have taken is that the principle of compulsory arbitration under law among nations would be effectual in the settlement of international disputes.
Of the 85 states that are parties to the statute today, 38 accept compulsory jurisdiction of the court but only 13 do so unconditionally or subject to the condition of reciprocity; nine do so subject to reciprocity or with respect to those disputes which arose after the declaration came into being or when other means of peaceful settlement have been employed by the parties; 16 apply more restrictive reservations. So far as Canada is concerned at the present time she reserves from the jurisdiction of the court only those disputes between members of the commonwealth of nations, those arising out of world

war II, and those that are of purely a domestic nature, the nature of which is decided upon by the court.
So far as the communist states are concerned, none of the communist states has accepted, nor have they given any indication that they will accept, compulsory jurisdiction. It is of interest, too, that the new states that are arising and coming into existence in Asia and Africa are following the same course. I believe that if we were able, among the nations of the world, with the will to achieve peace, to make stronger and more effective the international court of justice, giving it a compulsory jurisdiction and the right of compulsory decision, many of the problems we face today would be dissolved. There are difficulties in the way.
I think there are 16 members, and naturally nations are not given to trusting the courts that are set up. None the less if we in Canada, the United Kingdom, which has taken a very pronounced step forward in this regard, and the United States, which through the president has indicated that some additional powers should be given to the court, would lead in this direction I believe that ultimately the judgments of that court would commend themselves to the wisdom of mankind and we might well make a forward step toward the achievement of peace.
As a further step, I think that international action needs to be taken in respect of outer space. I mentioned that a moment ago. The principle is still in effect that each nation owns all the air above it. This principle was first declared in 1914 and re-declared in 1919. The principle has no efficacy today in this age, when even at the present moment several of these interstellar rockets are in circuit around the world. The existent principles of space law are out of date by reason of the scientific breakthroughs. We have gone a very considerable way in Canada in our willingness to bring about the attainment of an agreement on jurisprudence in outer space. The U.S.S.R. and other communist states refused to participate in the earlier committee. They are participating in the present one. I believe that if we could bring about international jurisdiction over space we would have gone a long way toward the preservation of mankind, not only in this generation but in the future. As a matter of priority we should have a declaration that would seem to be in keeping with reason, a declaration that no part of outer space or any celestial body may be appropriated by or may be subject to the jurisdiction of any particular nation.
The hon. member for Essex East advocated agreement on the elimination of weapons not now in existence. No doubt what he had in

mind was this problem of outer space and I hope that the outer space committee of the United Nations will be able to achieve a measure of agreement which will forestall the introduction of new weapons which use outer space.
I am not going to say more at this time The hon. gentlerhen asked, what general principles have you in mind. These are some principles that I believe contain more than a germ for the settlement of our international difficulties and for survival itself. I should have liked to have covered certain other matters that were dealt with, but as there is no possibility of agreement that we should go over to tomorrow to conclude this debate, I now conclude.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made this morning by the President of the United States of a new proposal-which will be discussed at the nuclear conference of three powers now under way in Geneva-together with the speech yesterday by Chairman Khrushchev to the

parliament of India in Delhi, emphasize the relevancy and the urgency of the position Canada should take in this all-important question, to use the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs disarmament.
The President's statement as announced this morning is that the United States is proposing to end forthwith, under assured controls, all nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, in the oceans, in those regions in space where effective controls can now be agreed on, and beneath the surface of the earth in cases where they can be monitored. Then the President made a significant observation, when he said the achievement of a workable nuclear test ban was by far the most important and difficult beginning to be made on the general subject of disarmament.
It is interesting to note that the position taken by Canada with regard to the unqualified banning of tests is to be contrasted in part with the proposal announced by the President of the United States, I do not need to spend needless time in justification of the consideration of disarmament in this debate.
I formed the impression after reading the minister's remarks this morning that, unintentionally, I am sure, he did convey the impression that this government was concerned with disarmament as its foremost objective. He also left the impression that not much had been done in this field in the period immediately preceding the time when hon. gentlemen opposite took over the responsibility of government in Canada.
That, of course, would be a wrong impression for anyone to have, because it will be recalled that almost at the very end of the war Canada and the government of that day, together with the friendly associated powers, did take immediate and comprehensive steps to bring about a solution to the problem of atomic armaments. In 1945 the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada offered to reciprocally share information concerning the practical application of atomic energy as soon as effective safeguards were devised against its use for destructive purposes. It will be remembered that at the first meeting of the United Nations Canada was made a member of the atomic energy commission. Following this joint declaration by the three heads of government, including Canada, there was presented a comprehensive, a most selfless plan for disarmament, and particularly nuclear disarmament, by the United States through Mr. Baruch, as the intermediary in the atomic energy commission.
It is important to remember what that proposal was. It suggested an international atomic development authority to which-
-would be entrusted all phases of the development and use of atomic energy, starting with the
External Affairs
raw material, with managerial control or ownership of all atomic energy activities potentially dangerous to world security, and power to control, license and inspect all other atomic activities, and which should itself be the world leader in the field of atomic knowledge and development so as to enable it to comprehend and therefore detect misuse of atomic energy.
The record now demonstrates that the Soviet union rejected this proposal and countered with one of its own, in which it was insisted that there should be an immediate prohibition of the use, production and accumulation of atomic weapons. That remained until 1954 the cardinal principle of Soviet policy on disarmament. There can be no doubt that the failure to make any progress in disarmament until 1955 was due, in my judgment, to the intransigence of the Soviet union with regard to this proposal and to its subsequent modifications, and other later proposals made by the western powers.
After 1955 the Soviet union did agree to a measure of international inspection and control, but never in specific and definable terms. The house will recall, too, that in 1954 the United Nations decided to create a subcommittee of the disarmament commission. As an indication of the interest Canada took in disarmament at that time, to the United States, Great Britain, France and the Soviet union as members of that committee was added the name of Canada.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) took part in the initial work of that subcommittee. If the subcommittee did not succeed-and it did not-the fault certainly was not that of Canada. The fault, generally speaking, was not that of the west, although I must say in an effort to be objective that the fault does not entirely rest on the Soviet union from that period on.
It is significant that France and Great Britain put forward at one of the early meetings of the subcommittee a comprehensive proposal for disarmament, a plan known as the Anglo-French plan. It was a three-stage disarmament scheme providing for a freeze on military establishments, in the first phase; for a second phase including the first half of agreed reductions in conventional forces and arms plus a cut-off on the production of nuclear weapons, and a final phase which was to see the completion of the remaining half of the agreed reductions of conventional arms. This was to be followed-and this was an answer to the Soviet union-by total prohibition and elimination of all nuclear weapons, and the conversion of all stocks to peaceful uses.
That memorandum represents one of the important landmarks in the discussions on disarmament. This Anglo-French initiative

External Affairs
was rejected by the Soviet union. It was supported by the United States and by Canada as members of the subcommittee.
In 1954 the then permanent delegate at the United Nations, Mr. Andre Vishinsky, made an important statement when he announced in the general assembly that the Soviet union had altered its traditional attitude. No longer would it insist on a ban on the manufacture and use and accumulation of atomic weapons as a condition precedent to entering into efforts to reach a solution on disarmament. And as a further evidence of the position of Canada in these discussions, the recognition of the useful role she had pursued, Canada was selected by the United States, France and Great Britain to carry on negotiations with the Soviet union which led to a resolution that stood in the name of the five powers and received the unanimous endorsa-tion of the general assembly of the United Nations.
Last night the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the resolution on disarmament put forward by the five great powers at the last assembly received unanimous support by all the United Nations, and he interpreted that as an indication of hope for the future.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out to the hon. member that I said it was cosponsored by all 82 nations.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. I do not want to be unfair to what my hon. friend said, but I would suggest that if that was an achievement-and it was merely a procedural resolution-so too was the achievement of 1954. But the significant point is that there was no constructive result arising from the unanimity. We should not draw unwarranted conclusions from unanimity on procedural resolutions, asserting that as a result we have cause to think we are now entering a more successful chapter in disarmament discussions. I hope we are, but I think it is well for us to curb our optimism with realism and give careful scrutiny to steps that may be taken which may represent more form than substance. Let us hope that the situation is otherwise.
It seems to me the next important step was the summit meeting in Geneva in 1954, when President Eisenhower, Sir Anthony Eden and Prime Minister Faure of France confronted Mr. Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev and when, as the result of a week's talk, four proposals on disarmament were put forward.
I would again suggest to hon. members that the spirit of Geneva that flowed from that summit meeting, giving hope as it did to all of the peoples of the world, has its counterpart

in the kind of possible false hope that could ensue as a result of discussions now under way. We must not be misled by generalizations of any kind. In our efforts to bring about disarmament we must recognize the value of a healthier international climate, but before giving final judgment we must see whether or not we have the acceptance of positions which we think are necessary for the maintenance of our security and for the successful pursuit of our objectives in the field of disarmament.
At this summit meeting a number of proposals were made, and for my present purposes the significant one was that put forward by President Eisenhower. He said to Mr. Khrushchev and Mr. Bulganin, "It is now scientifically impossible to detect undisclosed or secret nuclear weapons. You admitted that in discussions in the subcommittee only a few weeks ago. That being the case, since we cannot at present have full control on disarmament I make a proposal to you. Let us exchange our military blueprints. Let each give the other the opportunity of carrying out an aerial inspection survey in the territory of the other". The Soviet union did not accept that proposal. Canada was the one country, recognizing the scientific fact and the desirability of creating a, healthier international atmosphere, that did give support in principle to the Eisenhower proposal.
I think it is significant to note that as a result of the four-power meeting the subcommittee were instructed by the heads of the four governments to resume their discussions. They did not decide anything on disarmament. That was left once again to the subcommittee. It will be remembered that the subcommittee had its first meeting after the summit meeting on August 14, 1955. It will be remembered, too, that in September of that year the President of the United States suffered a serious heart seizure. From that moment on the Geneva spirit disappeared or dissipated. From that time forward there was no evidence of any progress, in spite of the good intentions and the healthy atmosphere that prevailed at the meetings in Geneva.
Canada at that time took a position, one that reflected the independence of Canada in foreign policy, as a result of the initiative and the character given that policy by the present Leader of the Opposition. We took the position that because we were apparently not able to resolve any of our differences, if we could not agree on some measure of disarmament on existing weapons, conventional or nuclear, could we not try to arrive at some agreement with respect to weapons

which were not then in existence? We of course had reference to the intercontinental ballistic missile.
It is not the fault of Canada-the record is there for everyone to see-that even more terrible weapons of war now confront us on an increasingly alarming scale. If our point of view had been pursued and accepted by all concerned it is possible that we would not be talking today of missiles that are capable of bringing about even greater destruction than other instruments of war.
This is perhaps what the Prime Minister was thinking about when at the general assembly in 1957 he said:
Experience has taught us that no country ever possesses a monopoly on any device. What one country has today, the other nations will have tomorrow, and the day is not far distant, if this continues, when there will be armouries of these rockets.
So we did take this position, even though it was a position which we alone took. We took another position. Because of the statement made by the President about the scientific fact precluding the complete control of undetected nuclear weapons, the United States reserved its position on all matters to which it had given its support up to that time. I -have referred to the Anglo-French memorandum of March, 1954 which was, apart from the Baruch plan, the first comprehensive proposal. The United States, through Mr. Harold Stassen, on September 6, 1955 stated:
The United States does now place a reservation upon all of its pre-Geneva substantive positions taken in this subcommittee, or in the disarmament commission, or in the United Nations on these questions in relationship to levels of armament.
Canada sought to persuade her -close and friendly associate in these matters that this was an unnecessary position to take, but other members of the subcommittee also took this position. The result wat that the agreement on manpower ceilings, the disarmament program produced by Britain and France, the 50 per cent arrangement about the cutoff, the 75 per -cent arrangement about the elimination of nuclear stocks, the detailed plan for inspection and control were all withdrawn. I believe that was at that time an unnecessary step. The Soviet union certainly did not make matters easy by taking the position it did with regard to bases and the like. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there -can be no doubt that during all of this period Canada has pursued, I believe diligently, its policy of trying, in concert with -other countries, to bring about an agreement on disarmament.
There was no want of independence; there was no reluctance to take a responsible position when it had to be taken, and I suggest to the Secretary of State for External
External Affairs
Affairs that if this is the important matter he says it is in current international affairs, Canada will have to do more than rely on its popularity as -a substitute for policy. Canada will have to do more than make generalizations with regard to this important matter if it wants to make the kind of contribution which I believe all of us want Canada to make at this time; and I am sure "all of us" includes the hon. gentleman who spoke yesterday. But I complained yesterday -and I think with some right-that in a matter of this sort, having in mind the importance which the hon. member attaches to this problem, it was regrettable that the government did not put forward some of its proposals or, at least, the principles on which those proposals are based.
I mentioned that Great Britain had taken that course in September. Chairman Khrushchev outlined the Soviet union proposals. Today we have the President of the United States making a proposal with regard to the banning of tests and saying that this is an essential prerequisite to a comprehensive system of disarmament, or to a system of partial disarmament. There are other proposals, namely the proposals put forward the other day by the French government, in which they emphasized the importance of controlling -production and the means of delivery of nuclear weapons.
