speechtext:
I think Canadians as a whole realize this. We all ought to have a degree of pride about this, not that spirit of disparagement which seemed now and then to creep into the remarks of the hon. gentleman. There should be pride in the fact that Canada today is being visited by leaders of all mankind. I speak of the visit of the prime minister of the Netherlands, the president of Mexico, the prime minister of the Ivory Coast, the Crown Prince and Princess of Ethiopia, the foreign minister of Norway, the defence minister of Germany, the prime minister and the foreign minister of Japan; I speak, also, of the forthcoming visits by the prime minister and the foreign minister of Italy, and later on, by the president of France, to whom the Leader of the Opposition referred in most laudatory terms; a man who represents in the view of Canadians as a whole, a land dear to our hearts and which is today facing conditions which all of us hope will be resolved in a degree of achievement in that nation which will raise her to even greater glories than in the past.
In other words, we live in an age of international exchange. Consultations are taking place with regularity.
Mention was made by the Leader of the Opposition of NATO. In so far as NATO is concerned we took a very strong stand last year that NATO must expand and advance along the course of collaboration, consideration and discussion. We took a stand against anything in the nature of a triumvirate or a council of NATO determining the course

External Affairs
of NATO. In other words, our attitude has been one desirous of the fullest consultation, without which none of the nations of the free world can achieve that unity without which there is no survival.
The same applies to the commonwealth, and I am not going to say more than a word with regard to the commonwealth. I listened to what the hon. gentleman had to say, and with much of his words in this regard I was in agreement-the tremendous part that is played by the varying parts of this commonwealth, the emergence and development of the commonwealth concept, and so forth. I saw something of the beginnings of this commonwealth in February of 1917, I think it was, when at the opening of the British parliament in that year the troops which escorted the reigning monarch to the opening ceremony were all troops of the Boers in the years 1897 to 1900. That was the beginning of the concept initiated by Jan Christian Smuts, using the words of an earlier day-the words of Rosebery in 1890:
The word "commonwealth" which in the passing years has resulted in an evolutionary process which continues unabated.
Both hon. gentlemen, the minister and the Leader of the Opposition, spoke of the commonwealth as a bridge between east and west, and I believe that. I am of those who believe that one of the major elements necessary to assure the fullest co-operation between the varying parts of the commonwealth is not any centralized authority, but through the medium of such organizations as the prime ministers' conference, the next one of which will be convened early in May. I go further than that, and say this: my belief is that the commonwealth prime ministers conference should as far as practicable meet once a year to the end that in a few days of discussion, while no decisions are finally made determinations may be arrived at of benefit not only to the peoples of the commonwealth but for mankind itself.
When one thinks of the conference of 1957, one realizes that out of that conference came the convening of a trade and economic conference which took place in the city of Montreal in September of 1958. Out of that conference came a system of commonwealth scholarships which in my opinion represent one of the most effective courses of action to unite the various parts of the commonwealth and remove those causes of difficulty because of colour and of race from which all mankind has suffered in every generation.
While mention was made a few moments ago by the Leader of the Opposition of the trade situation between Canada and the United States, I would point out that on January 7 this year the president of the board

of trade of the United Kingdom, the Right Hon. Mr. Maudling, emphasized the importance of expanding trade between Canada and the United Kingdom and spoke with satisfaction of the increase of British sales in Canada, expressing the hope of an expanding trade both ways. In other words, out of that conference came certain practical benefits for the people of this commonwealth.
This evening I intend to deal particularly with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I thought he made a most effective contribution to the subject before us on this occasion. Before I do so, however, and while it will not make for order-and order never arises out of a debating speech-I want to refer for just a moment to almost the concluding remarks of the Leader of the Opposition when he referred to the uranium situation.
I have read what has been said-and the hon. gentleman has re-emphasized it-to the effect that this government was responsible in some way for what is called the failure to secure an extension beyond 1962 of the contracts made by the former government. I believe I can do no better than to quote some of the remarks recorded in Hansard at the time which indicate that the hon. gentleman, a member of the then government, must not have realized the fact that the contracts entered into for uranium would terminate in 1962, and that there was not any indication that following that date governments would underwrite in any way the cost or the purchase of uranium. Agreements were entered into. They were gentlemen's agreements. The government of that day knew that when 1962 came that would be the end, to all intents and purposes, of this large export to the United States. I turn to the words of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe as reported at page 6440 of Hansard of July 20, 1955:
I know of no present shortage of uranium. Our production goes up steadily-
Then these words:
The situation is that no government is prepared to underwrite the purchase of uranium produced after 1962.
They knew that. Mr. Howe made it very clear. He then went on to say as reported at page 6441 of the same date:
I believe there will be a peacetime market for uranium. At that time the government will not be underwriting purchases.
I ask you, sir, who is responsible for the situation today, unfortunate as it is? The government of which the present Leader of the Opposition was a member realized that

in the agreements entered into after 1962 the government would not be underwriting purchases.
I turn now to the words of Mr. Howe as reported at page 1740 of Hansard of March 2, 1956:
The bulk of the uranium under contract goes to the atomic energy commission of the United States. When the contracts are completed, the contracts that are filed before the 31 March this year and approved by Canada and by the atomic energy commission we are informed that the foreseeable needs of the atomic energy commission of the United States for uranium from Canada will have been fulfilled.
Those three quotations from the words of Mr. Howe, the responsible minister, indicate that he knew that when 1962 came around those uranium contracts which provided so satisfactory an export would no longer be underwritten by governments. All that the last government did was to achieve some kind of an ephemeral gentlemen's agreement which said in effect that if everything goes all right everything will go all right with the export of uranium.
Now, the hon. member says, what did this government do? It made strong representations to the United States. In the intervening years not only has the demand for uranium gone down but indeed when one looks back over the years and examines the definition of uranium in the Encyclopedia Britannica, I believe in the 1920 edition, it is described as a valueless metal. Today we find ourselves in the position of having seen in the interventing years the United States engage in the production of its own uranium and demands for the metal are steadily decreasing.
When the Leader of the Opposition endeavours to pin responsibility on this government in that connection it is a case of the responsibility resting on him and his associates in the former administration for having failed to bring about when the contracts were entered into anything in the nature of a continuation after 1962.
What we did was this. Instead of having a cut-off date that would have put the uranium industry or a major portion of the business of this country out of business almost over night, we brought about a continuation of the contracts by a spread-over to the end that the sharpness of the termination of contracts would not bring about untoward sudden economic dislocation in the country.
I wish now to refer to the question of disarmament which was dealt with very thoroughly and completely by the hon. member for Essex East. He realized the difficulties of the problem. He realized the alterations in the perspective of mankind, the changes in a period of 15 years since the United Nations was founded, the discovery
External Affairs
and development of nuclear weapons, the tremendous power of emergent people all over the world to new sovereignties, the population explosion with its incalculable effects on this and succeeding generations, the scientific breakthrough and the ever-widening explorations of space. To meet this situation and these changing concepts new steps have to be taken. All of us search for an international institution that will resolve old and new conflicts, that will assure to mankind common security, welfare and international peace. These are no longer theoretical exercises of the mind, they are necessities for survival.
The hon. member for Essex East expressed the view that the government should place before parliament the representations it intends to make and has made regarding this problem of disarmament. The Leader of the Opposition says he does not want an independent course for Canada.

I intend to refer to one or two statements-

I do not know what these interruptions are. I listened to the hon. gentleman with patience, but he persists in those undertone interruptions, and I wish he would desist.
The hon. member for Essex East apparently believes that each nation should produce a collection of competing plans. What we believe is that there should be an agreed western position to serve as a point of departure in the negotiations with the U.S.S.R. in the 10-power talks which start next month in Geneva, and this is what we are aiming at: to make a contribution by the submission of proposals and comments which will assist in bringing about a plan for international disarmament which will be realistic, negotiable, and at the same time not imperil national security.
The hon. member for Essex East seemed to indicate that the United States was acting in such a way as not to assure that measure of agreement on this question which is the hope of mankind. Indeed, while he did not mention the United States in that connection when he spoke in Montreal on February 9 to the Canadian Club, he did say this, and I quote from the Montreal Star report:
Paul Martin outlines plan for disarmament.
Then, we find the following:
But Mr. Martin felt that the United States had also made a "great mistake" after the 1955 Geneva conference by being too adamant on its own program for disarmament and by tying in as well the settlement of political questions.
I agree with him that we should not join the settlement of political questions as such with the immediate problem of disarmament. I think that is of the essence, and that we should endeavour first by the ending of nuclear tests then by such measures of disarmament as are agreed to by stages to ensure that ultimately disarmament, the hope of mankind, will be attained.
Mention was made of the number of times that the question of disarmament has been discussed. The hon. gentleman went back to the days of Castlereagh, and he quoted from Sir Winston Churchill. I think one of the best epitomes of the whole problem of disarmament is to be found in the "Public Papers and Addresses" of Franklin D. Roosevelt, 1933. It is entitled, "An Appeal to the Nations of the World on the basis of disarmament and an end of economic chaos". Those words of 1933, which had the effect of mobilizing the thinking of mankind and the support of the nations, as evidenced by the replies that were made to this message did not, however, deny the outbreak of war six years later. These are some of the statements that the president made at that time. He said:

The disarmament conference has laboured for more than a year and, as yet, has been unable to reach satisfactory conclusions. Confused purposes still clash dangerously. Our duty lies in the direction of bringing practical results through concerted action based upon the greatest good to the greatest number. Before the imperative call of this great duty, petty obstacles must be swept away and petty aims forgotten. A selfish victory is always destined to be an ultimate defeat. The furtherance of durable peace for our generation in every part of the world is the only goal worthy of our best efforts.
Then, he sets out the plan and says:
If all nations will agree wholly to eliminate from possession and use the weapons which make possible a successful attack, defences automatically will become impregnable, and the frontiers and independence of every nation will become secure.
The ultimate objective of the disarmament conference must be the complete elimination of all offensive weapons. The immediate objective is a substantial reduction of some of these weapons and the elimination of many others.
You will remember, sir, the naval program of the 1920's, you will remember, sir, the Kellogg-Briand pact of 1926.

speechtext: It was 1928.

speechtext:
I recall very well when Mr. Mackenzie King, the then member for Prince Albert, came to Prince Albert for a couple of days and said he was on his way to Paris, and that in a few short days a pact would be signed there which would forever abolish war as an instrument for the settlement of disputes between the nations.
The Leader of the Opposition says that while peace is the aim and the purpose, we must not be fooled into believing that the events of recent months or years would lead us to expect that we are about to achieve that which mankind has tried for for generations. With these views I agree; none the less one must admit that in the last several months there has been an easing of tensions to such an extent that the hopes of mankind have been raised. The responsibility, therefore, on the part of those who have positions of international trust is the greater; for if we fail at this time, the potentialities for the future are certainly dark and grey.
While Mr. Khrushchev has been more conciliatory, he has also been most threatening. In the last speech he delivered in January, when he undertook to reduce the armed forces, he pointed out that they had an overwhelming supply of nuclear weapons. He used these words:
After the launching of soviet sputniks and rockets, the Americans have come to realize that the United States is no less vulnerable to attack than any other country.
Then, he went on to say:
The U.S.S.R. army has such arms as have heretofore been unknown to man.

Again, he said:
The U.S.S.R. has piled up such atomic and nuclear weapons and has powerful rocket equipment.
Then he promised the ultimate triumph, not by war but by economic destruction in the years ahead, for he said that the year 1959 was marked by success of the U.S.S.R. in the struggle for peace and the strengthening of the camp of socialism. He promised to reduce the numbers of men, but he ended up by saying that even when this is done his country will still be the most powerful in the world.
The hon. gentleman said that we should place before the House of Commons the actual representations that we have made or intend to make.

speechtext: What I said was that we should place before parliament our concepts in the form in which, for instance, the United Kingdom presented theirs, in the open and public assembly of the United Nations.

speechtext:
I accept that correction. The hon. member says that we should give a general idea of the concepts, if I understand him aright. I could summarize them in this way. These are views expressed in summary which I think represent the thinking of Canadians as a whole on this matter. First, Canada's policy should be directed to the achievement of maximum disarmament and the reduction of armed forces which can be verified and controlled without endangering the security of the nation against aggression.
Second, whatever is done cannot be achieved overnight and will require to be done by steps or stages. To that end I suggest that immediate consideration and priority might be given to the control of missiles designed to deliver nuclear weapons of mass destruction and also to bring about an agreement whereby the location of missile sites should be designated.
Third, at the conference at Pugwash much was said regarding biological and chemical weapons. I believe the time has come that the nations should agree that the manufacture and use of biological and chemical weapons should be banned.
Fourth, we come to the problem which transcends all these problems, namely that of outer space. If we are to preserve the future of mankind I believe that outer space should now, before further advances are made in its exploration, be declared banned to other than peaceful purposes and that the mounting of armaments on satellites should be outlawed. These are several suggestions that I think represent initial steps, for if there
External Affairs
is any desire on the part of the nations to bring about disarmament those principles could be accepted and I think should be accepted.
Now then you say, what about the production of fissile material for weapons? I think that was one of the questions asked. I would think that a major course leading to disarmament would be a declaration that the production of fissile material for weapons should be ended and that existing stocks should be transferred to peaceful uses as soon as a practical plan can be agreed upon. You say, what about the interim? You proceed by stages. What will you do in the meantime? How do you preserve the security of your state?
That brings me to one further step, and it is not a new one. It has been advanced since the 1600's that an international military force should be begun whose capability would be the restraining of nations from aggression. I digress for a moment to answer a statement made this afternoon by one hon. member who was filled with remorse, horror and shock that the government had not placed before the U.S.S.R. its willingness to set aside the Arctic areas of Canada to mutual inspection provided a like right was granted by the U.S.S.R. I first direct the attention of the house to my remarks on August 22, 1958. I do not want to spend long on this but I have to point out the fact that on that occasion I said, as found at page 3944 of Hansard:
For our part I can give unqualified assurances that to the extent that the control arrangements which may be agreed upon might be applicable to Canadian territory, we are prepared to co-operate in setting up control stations and inspection of the kind outlined in the report of the experts.
Apparently this was not read or, if read, not understood.
Indeed, on more than one occasion Canada has agreed unreservedly to her northern areas and Arctic regions being made available for inspection in order to ensure that surprise attacks will not take place.
These views have been communicated to Mr. Khrushchev on two occasions. The first was on January 18, 1958 when I wrote him and said this:
I give assurance that in the context of a disarmament agreement the Canadian government would be willing to open all or part of Canada to aerial and ground inspection on a basis of reciprocity. It seems to me that this is the type of proposal which should prove attractive to both our countries since we are neighbours across the Arctic. I have in mind in particular the kind of proposal Canada joined in sponsoring last August involving a system of inspection in the Arctic regions. We were willing then and are willing now to take such action in order to provide assurance against the fear of surprise attack.
This was turned down by Mr. Khrushchev in a subsequent letter or at least he 'did not

External Affairs
deal with the matter because he said we would have to have it as part of a world agreement. On May 9, 1958, I wrote to him in part as follows:
If you are really anxious about developments in the Arctic and if you wish to eliminate the possibility of surprise attack across the polar regions, I And it hard to understand why you should cast aside a proposal designed to increase mutual security in that area. Let me repeat here, Mr. Chairman, that we stand by our offer to make available for international inspection or control any part of our territory, in exchange for a comparable concession on your part. I would hope that you would accept some arrangement along these lines not only as an indication of our good faith but as part of a first, experimental step in building a system of international safeguards against surprise attack. When there is, by your own admission, a danger of nuclear war breaking out by accident or miscalculation, it is difficult for Canadians to comprehend your refusal to engage even in technical discussions intended to explore the feasibility of an international system of control.
That was Canada's stand.

speechtext: My time is limited. I am answering the hon. gentleman now. That was Canada's stand. That is the stand which we took not only in the United Nations but subsequently under the circumstances to which I have referred.

speechtext:
I doubt whether the hon. gentleman knows what bilateral means. Going on from there, and I hasten to conclude, I think that if the nations really desire to bring about disarmament and peace there is one field that could constitute an initial step, a course alongside one or other of the courses to which I have referred, and that is the acceptance of the jurisdiction of an international court of justice, the predecessor of which was the permanent court of international justice. All through the years the stand that we have taken is that the principle of compulsory arbitration under law among nations would be effectual in the settlement of international disputes.
Of the 85 states that are parties to the statute today, 38 accept compulsory jurisdiction of the court but only 13 do so unconditionally or subject to the condition of reciprocity; nine do so subject to reciprocity or with respect to those disputes which arose after the declaration came into being or when other means of peaceful settlement have been employed by the parties; 16 apply more restrictive reservations. So far as Canada is concerned at the present time she reserves from the jurisdiction of the court only those disputes between members of the commonwealth of nations, those arising out of world

war II, and those that are of purely a domestic nature, the nature of which is decided upon by the court.
So far as the communist states are concerned, none of the communist states has accepted, nor have they given any indication that they will accept, compulsory jurisdiction. It is of interest, too, that the new states that are arising and coming into existence in Asia and Africa are following the same course. I believe that if we were able, among the nations of the world, with the will to achieve peace, to make stronger and more effective the international court of justice, giving it a compulsory jurisdiction and the right of compulsory decision, many of the problems we face today would be dissolved. There are difficulties in the way.
I think there are 16 members, and naturally nations are not given to trusting the courts that are set up. None the less if we in Canada, the United Kingdom, which has taken a very pronounced step forward in this regard, and the United States, which through the president has indicated that some additional powers should be given to the court, would lead in this direction I believe that ultimately the judgments of that court would commend themselves to the wisdom of mankind and we might well make a forward step toward the achievement of peace.
As a further step, I think that international action needs to be taken in respect of outer space. I mentioned that a moment ago. The principle is still in effect that each nation owns all the air above it. This principle was first declared in 1914 and re-declared in 1919. The principle has no efficacy today in this age, when even at the present moment several of these interstellar rockets are in circuit around the world. The existent principles of space law are out of date by reason of the scientific breakthroughs. We have gone a very considerable way in Canada in our willingness to bring about the attainment of an agreement on jurisprudence in outer space. The U.S.S.R. and other communist states refused to participate in the earlier committee. They are participating in the present one. I believe that if we could bring about international jurisdiction over space we would have gone a long way toward the preservation of mankind, not only in this generation but in the future. As a matter of priority we should have a declaration that would seem to be in keeping with reason, a declaration that no part of outer space or any celestial body may be appropriated by or may be subject to the jurisdiction of any particular nation.
The hon. member for Essex East advocated agreement on the elimination of weapons not now in existence. No doubt what he had in

mind was this problem of outer space and I hope that the outer space committee of the United Nations will be able to achieve a measure of agreement which will forestall the introduction of new weapons which use outer space.
I am not going to say more at this time The hon. gentlerhen asked, what general principles have you in mind. These are some principles that I believe contain more than a germ for the settlement of our international difficulties and for survival itself. I should have liked to have covered certain other matters that were dealt with, but as there is no possibility of agreement that we should go over to tomorrow to conclude this debate, I now conclude.

speechtext: May I speak to a point of order? If the minister is rising now to conclude the debate, he has not very much time and I am sure we on this side would be very happy to continue to sit until he has had every opportunity to deal with the points raised.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The members of this group, because of the importance of the questions that are being considered in this debate and the great concern of the Canadian people with these problems, welcome the proposal of the Prime Minister for the continuation of this debate tomorrow but we are not ready to sit after 10 o'clock this evening.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have two proposals. The Prime Minister has invited the house to modify the order which was made earlier that this debate should conclude at 10 o'clock. If there is no possibility of a general agreement on that-

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We are prepared to continue the debate tomorrow.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I point out what may not be known to some hon. gentlemen, namely that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), and the hon. member for Essex East, (Mr. Martin), who have taken a prominent part in this debate, would like to hear it concluded but they made other arrangements because of the order of business. subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What would happen if the two members died, would the house close?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, without submitting the house to the dire possibility envisaged by the hon. gentleman, could we not agree to the debate next Tuesday when the hon. gentlemen will be back?

speechtext: That is agreeable.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I take it that would not interfere with the continuation of the supply debate? Perhaps Wednesday would be a better time because we have a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We are not counting on a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday. Monday would be private members' day.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: If Monday is private members' day-of course it is up to the house to decide-we would have no objection. We were under the impression, from the leader of the house, that Monday was going to be a supply day and we have been operating on that basis.

speechtext: The Prime Minister indicated that last night.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I so indicated it was not through direct statement. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the house prepared to agree unanimously to the extension of this debate to Tuesday and that it be concluded on Tuesday?

speechtext: Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On Friday we will continue with the supplementary estimates. If they are concluded tomorrow we will take these items in this order: the resolution in the name of the Minister of Justice to amend the Department of Justice Act; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport to amend the Railway Act; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works to amend the National Housing Act. Then in the unlikely event of this business being concluded tomorrow, we will take Bill No. C-2, to amend the Indian Act and Bill No. C-3, to amend the Canada Elections Act. That will be the business for Friday. Monday will be private members' day. That is the second Monday of six Mondays for that purpose. Tuesday we have now agreed will be devoted to a continuation of the debate on external affairs in which we were engaged today. Should that debate draw to a close before ten o'clock we would take any item of government business that I have now outlined for Friday. On Wednesday there would be a continuation of government business, the items to be announced later. Thursday of next week will be the second Thursday as a private members' day and will be devoted to the discussion of the measure relating to capital punishment.
May I ask the house leader whether it is intended that debate should last for the one day only? I refer to the debate on capital punishment which he has suggested for Thursday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
With regard to the debate on capital punishment, may I say this. I endeavoured to get an agreement in the usual manner and a conclusion was not reached as to whether that debate should proceed beyond that one day. The best suggestion I have heard is that as the debate proceeds on that Thursday we should attempt to arrive at a decision then as to whether another day would be required. Unless I hear further from the other parties in the house, the only information I have at the moment is

that there will be just the one day for that particular debate. However, I am open to suggestions.

On that particular point may I say a word. The house leader said he had not been able to get any information from this side of the house as to what our intentions are in respect of this debate. As far as this party is concerned, we shall be glad to give the house leader our views when he confronts us with some of the intentions and views of the government with respect to this matter. It is surely the responsibility of the government to let us know what they wish to do and then ask our views but not to ask our views so that we may be put in the position of accepting or rejecting a particular course, of action before we know what the views of the house leader and the government are.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot be placed in this position by the Leader of the Opposition without protesting. That is not the case whatsoever. I consulted with the house leader of his party with regard to this matter on the most congenial of terms, in the same manner as I always get on with him in these matters. The matter was left open as to what the opposition desired to do. The impression I gathered from him was that he was not sure what their plan was. Hence the matter is open and continues to be open for negotiation. It is not a settled matter by any means. I did not at any time suggest that the matter was closed.
Would the house leader now, while we are talking about this matter, tell us the desire and the views of the government with regard to how this question should be handled in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know whether we can do it here by way of public debate. The other group has been consulted as well. As I say, there is a difference of opinion at the moment as to what should transpire concerning this particular debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No order is needed to proceed with the proposed business on Thursday because it seems to be the first item under public orders. Perhaps the different interests could arrive at some conclusion, if it is possible, between now and the time the debate concludes.
